title: [CNCF] Is your OpenTelemetry pipeline becoming a performance bottleneck?
summary: At Cloud Native Days Austria 2026, I presented a talk called How to Defeat OTel’s Silent Killer: The Performance Overhead, exploring a problem that is easy to overlook when building observability pipelines: the cost of collecting telemetry itself. OpenTelemetry has become a cornerstone of cloud-native observability, providing standardized APIs, SDKs, and tooling for generating, collecting, processing, and exporting metrics, logs, and traces. However, instrumentation and telemetry processing are not free. Every span created, attribute attached, and batch exported consumes resources. As applications scale, poorly configured telemetry pipelines can introduce significant CPU usage, memory pressure, network traffic, and storage costs. In some cases, the infrastructure responsible for observing a system can become a performance problem of its own. The good news is that much of this overhead can be understood, measured, and reduced without sacrificing the visibility engineers depend on. Where does OpenTelemetry overhead come from? When discussing OpenTelemetry performance, we often focus on the application SDK. However, the cost extends beyond instrumentation. The entire telemetry pipeline contributes to resource consumption, from generating spans and collecting metrics to processing, exporting, and storing data. Instrumentation overhead is also workload-dependent. Two applications using the same instrumentation libraries can experience very different results depending on request throughput, attribute volume, runtime behavior, and the number of spans generated per request. This is why relying on a single overhead percentage can be misleading. Instead, we should examine CPU consumption, memory usage, application latency, telemetry volume, and the behavior of the Collector under load. There is also an important trade-off between application safety and telemetry completeness. When a pipeline becomes overloaded, backpressure and memory safeguards can protect the application and OpenTelemetry Collector, but they may also lead to rejected or dropped telemetry. The objective is not simply to minimize resource consumption. It is to maintain useful observability while keeping its operational cost predictable. Investigating the Collector: five common configuration problems For my demonstration, I used Telemetrygen, an OpenTelemetry utility that generates synthetic telemetry, to investigate how Collector configuration affects resource consumption. The investigation focused on five common sources of unnecessary overhead. 1. Inefficient batching Exporting small amounts of telemetry frequently can increase serialization work, export requests, and network overhead. The OpenTelemetry Collector groups telemetry inside the exporter’s sending queue before transmitting it downstream, helping amortize this work across larger payloads. (Note: Historically, this was handled by a standalone batch processor, which is now deprecated in favor of built-in exporter batching). However, batching parameters should reflect the actual workload. Larger batches are not automatically better: they can increase buffering requirements and affect export latency. exporters: otlp_grpc: endpoint: "otel-backend:4317" sending_queue: enabled: true sizer: items queue_size: 100000 batch: enabled: true min_size: 8192 flush_timeout: 200ms Configuring batch inside an exporter’s sending_queue groups spans, metrics, or logs before forwarding them downstream, improving compression efficiency and durability while reducing export overhead. Batches are sent when a configured size threshold is reached or a timeout expires. In this example, min_size: 8192 triggers an export when the batch reaches 8,192 items, while flush_timeout: 200ms triggers an export regardless of batch size. Once batching is enabled, these values are the Collector’s documented defaults, not universal performance recommendations. (Note: Because unbatched requests enter the queue first in this architecture, this example switches sizer from the default requests to items with a queue_size of 100000 to prevent smaller, unbatched bursts from overflowing the queue). The important point is to measure how batching affects resource consumption and throughput rather than relying on example configurations. 2. Unnecessary resource attributes Resource attributes provide valuable context about the systems producing telemetry. But collecting and forwarding attributes that nobody uses can increase payload sizes and downstream processing costs. For example, an application might need host.name, host.arch, and os.type for troubleshooting, but not detailed hardware information such as host.cpu.model.name or host.cpu.cache.l2.size. The OpenTelemetry Collector’s resource detection processor allows engineers to configure which system attributes are collected. Disabling unnecessary attributes can reduce telemetry volume and processing overhead, although the impact on storage and cardinality depends on the backend. A practical example: Keep the hostname and operating system type, but disable CPU model and cache metadata when those details are not needed for troubleshooting. 3. Aggressive receiver polling Infrastructure receivers collect metrics at configured intervals, often independently of application traffic. Polling host metrics, container statistics, databases, and network services every few seconds creates continuous work even when applications are relatively idle. Increasing collection intervals from 10 to 30 seconds, where operational requirements permit, can reduce collection frequency and associated overhead. This introduces a trade-off: lower polling frequency means less temporal resolution. The appropriate interval depends on how quickly a metric changes and how it is used for troubleshooting or alerting. 4. Exporting every trace Not every successful request needs to produce a trace that is retained. Exporting all traces can consume significant bandwidth, Collector resources, and backend capacity, particularly in high-throughput applications. Sampling provides a way to control this volume. Head-based sampling makes decisions early, reducing downstream work. Tail-based sampling makes decisions after observing more of a trace, enabling policies that retain errors or other diagnostically interesting requests. These policies retain traces with an error status and probabilistically sample 5% of traces, including potentially some additional error traces. However, tail sampling is not free. It requires buffering trace data until a decision can be made, introducing additional memory and processing overhead. Choosing a sampling strategy means balancing cost, diagnostic value, and the resources needed to make sampling decisions. 5. Memory safeguards applied too late The OpenTelemetry Collector includes a memory_limiter processor to help manage memory pressure. Processor ordering matters. When enrichment and transformation processors run before memory limiting, the Collector may perform additional work on telemetry that is subsequently refused under memory pressure. Memory limiting is a protective mechanism rather than a performance optimization in itself. Its purpose is to improve stability under pressure, not necessarily to reduce CPU consumption during normal operation. Placing the memory limiter early in the pipeline helps apply safeguards before more expensive processing. It is important to understand that the memory limiter is not a substitute for appropriate resource limits or capacity planning. It can refuse incoming data when memory pressure becomes excessive, and receivers must handle this behavior correctly to avoid unnecessary telemetry loss. From local experiments to production architecture Optimizing a single Collector is only part of the solution. In Kubernetes, telemetry workloads can fluctuate significantly as applications scale, deployments change, and traffic increases. A Collector configuration that performs well under synthetic load may behave differently in production. Here are some architectural practices that can help address these challenges. Separate collection from centralized processing. A two-tier architecture can use lightweight edge Collectors for local collection and gateway Collectors for more expensive processing. This allows different parts of the pipeline to scale according to their workloads. Control telemetry volume early. Filtering unnecessary attributes, removing unneeded data, and avoiding excessive cardinality can reduce the amount of information processed and transferred downstream. These decisions should preserve the context required for debugging and correlation. Plan for memory pressure and backend outages. Kubernetes memory limits, Collector memory safeguards, bounded queues, and retry mechanisms serve different purposes. Persistent queues can improve resilience during temporary backend failures, but they still require capacity planning and cannot guarantee delivery under every failure scenario. Scale with signal-specific requirements in mind. Horizontal scaling can increase throughput, but stateful processing requires additional consideration. Tail sampling, for example, generally requires spans belonging to the same trace to reach the same processing instance. These architectural decisions are just as important as tuning individual processors. Don’t forget the instrumentation One of the most effective optimizations happens before telemetry reaches the Collector. Instrumentation should answer meaningful operational questions rather than collect everything simply because it is possible. Excessive spans, high-cardinality attributes, and unnecessary instrumentation can increase resource consumption throughout the entire pipeline. For metrics, attributes containing unbounded values such as unique request IDs can create large numbers of distinct time series. For traces and logs, excessive attributes and events increase payload sizes and may affect backend processing or indexing costs. Why I chose Telemetrygen for my demo When preparing my performance investigation, I initially considered using the official OpenTelemetry Astronomy Shop. While it is an excellent environment for exploring instrumentation across microservices, its multiple applications, databases, and supporting services introduce additional CPU and memory consumption. For this experiment, I wanted to isolate the Collector’s performance overhead without the background noise of a complete application environment. Instead, I chose Telemetrygen, a lightweight utility for generating synthetic traces, metrics, and logs at controlled rates. In my OpenTelemetry performance overhead demo, I used synthetic telemetry to investigate how Collector configuration affects resource consumption. The demonstration walks through common inefficiencies, including missing batching, unnecessary resource attributes, aggressive receiver polling, excessive trace export, and memory limiter placement, showing how targeted configuration changes can improve pipeline efficiency. This approach helped isolate Collector behavior, but it is only one part of the performance picture. For understanding instrumentation overhead inside real applications, a complete environment such as Astronomy Shop remains valuable. Exploring instrumentation further Reducing overhead starts with understanding what telemetry an application generates and why. The official OpenTelemetry instrumentation documentation introduces automatic and manual instrumentation, while the sampling documentation explains how to control trace volume. These are useful starting points for reviewing instrumentation decisions before optimizing the Collector itself. For engineers interested in investigating performance further, the OpenTelemetry Collector documentation covers pipeline configuration and processing. The OpenTelemetry community is also a good place to discuss performance challenges. The Collector SIG focuses on Collector architecture, performance, and configuration, with discussions taking place in the #otel-collector channel on CNCF Slack. For questions about instrumentation overhead in a specific programming language, the corresponding language SIG is a better starting point. The OpenTelemetry community page provides information about SIGs, public meetings, and how to get involved. Making performance part of observability design OpenTelemetry overhead is not a single problem with a single configuration fix. It is the combined effect of instrumentation decisions, data volume, processor configuration, export behavior, and infrastructure architecture. The most useful lesson from this investigation is that observability pipelines should be measured and optimized like any other production system. Start with controlled benchmarks. Understand where resources are consumed. Introduce configuration changes individually, and evaluate their impact on CPU, memory, latency, throughput, and telemetry loss. Most importantly, treat example configurations as starting points rather than production-ready defaults. OpenTelemetry gives us the tools to understand complex distributed systems. With thoughtful instrumentation, careful pipeline configuration, and appropriate scaling strategies, we can ensure that collecting this information does not become an unnecessary burden on the systems we are trying to observe.

title: [Netflix] Engineering AI Discover
summary: The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layerBy Varun Khaitan, Peng Ren, Gary Tang, Itay Teller, Atif Faheem, Nipun Kumar, Donnie DeBoer, Eduardo Lundgren, Matteo Rinaldi, Raghav BakshiWe recently introduced AI Discover, a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see.Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? Our answer is a new intelligence layer, the agent harness behind AI Discover. For each request, it decides how to combine LLMs with our recommendation systems. It builds on years of work understanding what members enjoy, and on our recent work applying LLMs to recommendations and generative experiences. The layer itself plans each request, runs it across those systems, serves the result and evaluates it offline.This post covers the challenges we designed for and the key decisions we made along the way.Why an intelligence layer?Every Netflix page combines recommendations with rules. We pick titles a member may enjoy, and eligibility, maturity and safety rules decide what can appear. An experience built on LLMs needs the same rules, plus code that decides when to call an LLM and how to handle its output. That code is called an agent harness, and it’s the core of our intelligence layer.The simplest implementation hands the entire request to an LLM and lets it pick the titles, write the labels and decide what happens next. However, that leaves us relying on probabilistic output where we need governed results, because every turn in AI Discover ends on a screen in someone’s living room. At our scale, even rare failures happen many times a day. A member sees every slow call, unavailable title or off-brand line. Seven challenges shaped our design:Fitting LLMs into a product and architecture designed without them. Traditional recommenders rank titles based on past behavior. LLMs can do more: understand what a member is asking for and plan how to respond. Our existing experience would leave most of that unused.Keeping recommendations grounded. Every pick must be a real, available title from our changing catalog. Retrieval and rankers work in tandem with LLMs to choose titles that fit the member’s taste and intent.Working with slow, unpredictable LLMs. LLM calls are the slowest and most expensive part of the system. Tail latencies can spike, and the output may not be what you asked for. So we use LLMs selectively, treat what they return as untrusted input and test performance and quality before anything ships.Adapting to fast-changing models, tools and prompts. Modeling and engineering solutions keep evolving, so the product can’t depend on any single model, tool or prompt.Building for TV. Typing on a TV is hard, so members rely on the remote, and the app should respond to every press right away on widely varying hardware. TV apps also update slowly, so changes have to ship without an app release. A typical TV request returns in moments, while multi-step generation can take several seconds.Holding a safety and reliability bar at scale. Members always get a page, even when an LLM call fails or yields poor results. Their choices and our content standards hold on every request, and when something breaks, structured records show why.Learning from what members say alongside what we already know. Recommendations have always learned from viewing behavior. AI Discover also lets members tell us what they want, and that has to shape what they see next.System ArchitectureWhen a member picks a theme, the TV app sends the request to the Page Server, which builds pages for all Netflix apps and hands the request asynchronously to the intelligence layer. At a high level, this new layer has two components: a controller and an executor.The controller decides what to run. It gathers the context needed for each request, including real-time signals such as the time of day. It then settles on a plan, either an established one or a new one drafted by its planner, validates it and retrieves only the member details that this plan requires from Memory Hub, our per-member memory store. These details may include member taste summaries generated by MemberLLM, our in-house language model for personalized recommendations, or feedback shared by the member. We talk more about Memory Hub and member taste summaries later.A plan is a graph of approved steps, each running a capability. A capability is a named unit of work that can have multiple versions and belongs to a family such as retrieval, ranking, generation or packaging. It declares its inputs and outputs, the context it may see and what happens if it fails.Capability declarations make a plan verifiable. Before execution, the controller validates the graph: every step is approved, every input has a producer, nothing loops and the plan ends in exactly one page. Afterward, the controller checks the result before it’s served.The executor runs the plan. Steps pass typed outputs to each other through the declared contracts, so each receives exactly what it asked for. Independent steps run in parallel, each with its own deadline and appropriate fallback behaviors. Some steps are optimized LLM calls with one task each, such as writing row titles or suggesting next themes, and they act only within the validated plan. Checks before the run and contracts during it give us governed execution, where every action stays within limits set in code.Both parts write to the request records, the traces we use offline to evaluate and improve the system.System Architecture DiagramKey DecisionsEach challenge led to one decision. Here’s what we chose and what it bought us.1. Design the product and architecture around LLMsWe reimagined the experience around LLMs. The easier path would have been to drop them in as rankers, keep today’s latency budgets and precompute where necessary. AI Discover is built on a back-and-forth around themes a member can steer, which gives LLMs work only they can do: generating themes, explaining rows, summarizing taste and helping choose the titles that fit the member and the moment. Members pick themes with the remote, so they never have to type. On the TV, those themes and explanations get their own native UI elements. Behind the screen, LLMs can draft plans, and asynchronous serving gives multi-step agentic orchestration the time it needs.This opens up experiences our traditional stack couldn’t support on its own.2. Make existing systems composableKeeping recommendations grounded meant building on the systems that already know our catalog and members. Most capabilities wrap complex, proven Netflix systems such as search, large-scale ranking and catalog metadata access. Some of them may run their own agents in the future.Reshaping them took careful work, because agentic orchestration challenges many long-standing assumptions of distributed systems. A capability now has to work in combinations no one designed, for a caller that chooses to call it at runtime. Each one needs a clear purpose and a semantic interface, and shaping it means deciding how much to combine into a single step and how much to leave to the planner. Too fine, and the planner has more ways to go wrong; too coarse, and it loses room to compose richer plans.In return, the planner gets building blocks it can mix in new ways, and connecting services takes far less manual wiring. Because plans can only use these blocks, even one drafted on the fly stays grounded in our catalog and member taste.3. Plan first, then executeTo contain LLM latency and errors, we plan every request before anything runs. The familiar way to let an agent use tools is a loop: reason, call a tool, read the result, reason again. It’s flexible, but you can’t tell up front how many steps it will take or whether it has gone down a wrong path. In agent terms, ours is a plan-and-execute agent: an LLM can propose the path, but code decides whether it runs.Plans come from two places: established plans we’ve already tested, and plans an LLM drafts on the fly. A router we control decides which one is served. Either way, the plan passes the same checks before it runs. If the planner is slow or its plan fails a check, we fall back to a tested plan.This allows for adaptive planning. The planner can find new ways to serve a request, and we can balance cost, latency and quality for each task, from a lean single-call plan to a richer multi-step one.4. Stay model and capability agnosticThe best model or capability for a task today may be second-best, or overkill, in a few months, so we built the system to switch between them. We assign each task to the model or capability version that fits it. Today that’s a per-task setting we can override live. Only some steps in a request use an LLM.That only works if switching is easy. All the LLMs we use sit behind one common interface. Before we switch, each candidate is scored on the same tasks by automated checks and LLM judges, so every swap is a measured change.Much of the system’s behavior lives in server-side prompts and configuration, so we can swap models, tools and capabilities without new code or a TV app release.Upgrades get cheap and experiments get easy. Moving to a better model, ranker or retrieval system is a plan or setting change, not a migration, so each component can keep improving without a large investment.5. Make page generation asynchronousInference keeps getting faster, but member expectations rise just as quickly: richer responses, more context and more of the page shaped by LLMs. The line between what feels instant and what’s worth waiting for will keep shifting, so we built the asynchronous path as a first-class way of serving.Most of a TV app is synchronous: press a button, get a page. Generative work breaks that pattern. Holding one request open for many seconds across services would tie up too many threads. So requests that involve generation are asynchronous. The press returns right away with an acknowledgement, and the TV switches to a thinking state that explains what’s being prepared. Meanwhile, the executor runs the plan in the background. When the result is ready, the server notifies the TV, which then fetches it.Slow generation no longer slows anything else. The serving path stays healthy however long a turn takes, and every press still gets immediate feedback on screen.Async Sequence Diagram6. Enforce safety in codeSome rules must hold no matter what an LLM writes: content and maturity standards, what each step can access, and what a member has asked us not to show them. Putting those rules in a prompt makes them probabilistic, so we enforce them in code. Generated text is cleaned up before it reaches the screen. The planner sees a stripped-down request, and member details are limited to what the validated plan needs.For example, the planner decides which inputs each step needs, such as the profile’s maturity rating for retrieval. Instead of writing parameter values directly, it uses placeholders. After the plan passes validation, the controller fills them with values from the request, matched by declared type. This also protects against prompt injection.Each request also leaves a structured record: the plan, each step and its outcome, and which rules applied. When a page misses, we can tell whether the plan, the data, a rule or the model was at fault. The same records feed our offline evaluation and replay.Together, these rules and records let an experiment ship at the same safety and privacy bar as the rest of the product.7. Remember what members tell usA taste summary is a short profile of what a member enjoys, such as favorite genres, tone and recurring themes. MemberLLM generates it ahead of time from the member’s viewing history, which keeps that LLM work off the request path. It helps us further personalize their page, and steps that write themes and explanations receive it as context, so their wording reflects the member. We’ll cover MemberLLM in more detail in an upcoming post.In AI Discover, members can also tune their recommendations and tell us directly what they want. Those choices apply right away and carry across visits, and they give us a new signal alongside what we already know about their taste. This is a first step toward remembering more about each member, from their preferences to the habits that show up over time and the corners of the catalog they like to explore. We keep it all in Memory Hub, our persistent, low-latency memory store, next to their taste summaries, and we can add new kinds of memory as we need them. We apply these memories to later requests where they’re relevant, together with real-time context.The member holds the remoteIn this version, members interact by selecting themes and using tuning options such as “don’t recommend.” There’s no free-text input or open-ended chat. That keeps the LLM’s job narrow by design.The usual protections still apply. Profile settings and our safety and privacy policies hold here as everywhere else.Generated text was tested before launch. We ran safety evaluations on theme labels, row titles and explanations to make sure they meet our standards.What’s nextIt would have been faster to let an LLM do everything and stop there. The intelligence layer gave us an AI-native product, grounded building blocks, adaptive planning, quicker experimentation, asynchronous generation, governed execution and agent memory for tunable personalization. While AI Discover is its first experience, we designed it with more in mind.We’ve organized our efforts to answer two questions:How much do members want to shape their recommendations? Whether they’d rather steer or lean back, and how much, which kinds of themes help, and how we should blend what members tell us with our existing personalization systems.What tradeoffs does this technology bring? How cost and latency hold up in production as we ramp traffic, how long members will wait for generated results, and whether errors came from the model, the harness or our existing systems. Multi-turn sessions also need different evaluation and observability than single requests.Longer term, our goal is a system that improves itself, starting from the record each request leaves behind. Today we replay past requests against a new prompt, model or rule to see what changes, and we judge each change with automated checks, LLM judges and human evaluations. Eventually, we want the system to propose improvements, test them safely and keep only what proves better, within our privacy and data-use policies. As LLMs improve, more of the work may move into them, and the intelligence layer lets us move that line deliberately.This is part of a bigger shift. Recommendation systems have long learned quietly from what members watch and answered with ranked rows. LLMs let them listen and respond, and members may increasingly expect that. We’ll keep exploring what that means for discovery on Netflix.AcknowledgementsWe would like to thank Adi Suresh, Akash Katipally, Allan Johns, Becks Wood, Bhargav Mangipudi, Carrie Santiago, Chris Martin, Claire Campbell, Corey Waldin, Dana Sittler, Daneo Zhang, David Leen, Devon Bryant, Dharamendra Kumar, Dharini Chandrasekaran, Ebony Turner, Federico Roa, Gianfranco Cuoco, Guru Tahasildar, Haley Clanton, Haresh Chudgar, Ivan Provalov, James Schultz, JingXu Yang, Josie Shaw, Kamelia Aryafar, Kate Cummings, Kathleen Garrity, Kelley Robinson, Kevin Du, Kevin O’Connor, Kyla Moore, Kyle Lind, Laura Matsuura, Leah Cusella, Lingyi Liu, Lingyong Wang, Mallory Walkup, Matthew Pereira, Michael Galassi, Minsu Jang, Moumita Bhattacharya, Paran Jain, Paul Lee, Qusai Al-Rabadi, Scarlet Chen, Sergi Perez, Sriram Rao, Stephen Shaw, Sura Elamurugu, Varad Pathak, Yesu Feng, Zainab Mahar Mir, and Zhongli Cheng for their contributions to this work.Engineering AI Discover was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Kubernetes] Kubernetes v1.38 Sneak Peek
summary: As we get closer to the release date for Kubernetes v1.38, the project develops and matures, features may be deprecated, removed, or replaced with better ones for the project's overall health. This blog post outlines some of the planned changes for the Kubernetes v1.38 release that the release team feels you should be aware of for the continued maintenance of your Kubernetes environment and keeping up to date with the latest changes. The information listed below is based on the current status of the v1.38 release and may change before the actual release date. Deprecations and removals for Kubernetes v1.38kubectl: WebSocket opt-out environment variables removedkubectl has used WebSockets instead of SPDY by default for kubectl exec, attach and cp since v1.30, and for kubectl port-forward since v1.31. The KUBECTL_REMOTE_COMMAND_WEBSOCKETS and KUBECTL_PORT_FORWARD_WEBSOCKETS environment variables let you turn that behavior off. These variables are going to be removed in v1.38. kubectl will then always try WebSockets first and fall back to SPDY when it needs to (the same as the current default behavior). If your scripts or CI environments set either of these environment variables, you can remove them since they will no longer have any effect. To learn more, refer to KEP-4006: Transition from SPDY to WebSockets. kubectl: name dropped from kuberc credential plugin allowlist entriesThe kuberc file keeps kubectl user preferences separate from cluster credentials in the kubeconfig, including an allowlist of the credential plugins kubectl is allowed to run. In the beta kubectl.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 API, an allowlist entry can use name as an alias for command. The name field (not command) has been deprecated since v1.36. With kuberc expected to graduate to stable in v1.38, the new kubectl.config.k8s.io/v1 API will not include name. If any of your allowlist entries use name, change them to command now. To learn more, refer to KEP-3104: Separate kubectl user preferences from cluster configs. Ongoing major changesFuture removal of cgroup v1 supportSupport for cgroup v1 is being phased out. Since v1.35, the kubelet fails to start on nodes that use cgroup v1 unless you set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration. This option remains available in v1.38, but it should be treated as a short-term fix as support for cgroup v1 is planned to be removed in a future release. If you haven't already, please plan your migration to cgroup v2. To learn more, refer to KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support. Admission webhooks no longer receive authentication and authorization review requestsSince v1.37, the ExcludeAdmissionWebhookVirtualResources feature gate has been enabled by default. With it on, validating and mutating admission webhooks no longer receive requests for (virtual) writes to TokenReview, SelfSubjectReview, SubjectAccessReview, SelfSubjectAccessReview, LocalSubjectAccessReview or SelfSubjectRulesReview. Creating or updating a webhook configuration whose rules name one of these resources returns a deprecation warning, and the API server logs any existing configurations that are affected when it starts. If you rely on a webhook to see these requests, you can turn the feature gate off for now, but note that the gate is planned to be locked on when the feature graduates to stable. To learn more, refer to KEP-5793: Manifest Based Admission Control Config. Breaking changes in Kubernetes v1.38Container runtimes must report the cgroup driverThe kubelet in v1.37 and older supported releases provides a legacy mechanism to configure the cgroup driver. The modern way to do that is via the CRI RuntimeConfig RPC, which reports the cgroup driver that the container runtime recommends using. In v1.38, the kubelet defaults to not allowing the legacy configuration mechanism: it will be both deprecated and unavailable unless explicitly re-activated. As a result, v1.38 nodes will essentially require that your container runtime is running before the kubelet starts (to look up the expected cgroup driver); if the kubelet can't get the cgroup driver from the runtime even after retrying, it will exit with an error before even registering the node. As part of this upcoming release, the cgroupDriver field in the kubelet configuration file will be deprecated. Not only is specifying that field going to be deprecated, the kubelet will actually reject it unless you reactivate the legacy mechanism by enabling the (temporary) LegacyCgroupDriverFallback feature gate. The kubeadm tool will also no longer set cgroupDriver to systemd by default, and its preflight checks will report an error if the runtime doesn't support the RPC. If any of your nodes run an older, incompatible container runtime, you should follow the instructions in the official v1.38 release notes about how to upgrade. To learn more, refer to KEP-4033: Discover cgroup driver from CRI and kubernetes/kubernetes#136731. Pod-level resources: swap behavior changes on LimitedSwap nodesIf you use pod-level resources on Linux nodes that use cgroup v2 and are configured with LimitedSwap, the kubelet in v1.38 will start applying swap limits based on the Pod's pod-level memory settings. This means that Pods whose pod-level memory request equals their memory limit will get no swap at all (both for the Pod and for every container in it), even if a container sets a memory request lower than its limit. Check any workloads that rely on swap before you upgrade, and be sure to read the official release notes for v1.38 for detailed advice. To learn more, refer to KEP-2837: Pod Level Resource Specifications. Featured enhancements of Kubernetes v1.38The following list of enhancements is likely to be included in the upcoming v1.38 release. This is not a commitment and the release content is subject to change. kubectl user preferences (kuberc) graduating to stablekuberc, the separate kubectl configuration file for user preferences such as aliases, default options and a credential plugin policy, is expected to graduate to stable in v1.38. To learn more, read Kubectl user preferences (kuberc) or refer to KEP-3104: Separate kubectl user preferences from cluster configs. Pod-level resources graduating to stablePod-level resources, which let you set CPU, memory and hugepages requests and limits for a Pod as a whole, are expected to graduate to stable in v1.38. If you run Linux nodes with LimitedSwap, see the swap behavior change above before you upgrade. To learn more, read Assign Pod-level CPU and memory resources or refer to KEP-2837: Pod Level Resource Specifications. DRA support for partitionable devices graduating to stablePartitionable devices let a Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) driver advertise a device such as a GPU both as a whole and as smaller partitions, and the scheduler allocates only combinations that fit within the physical device. The feature is expected to graduate to stable in v1.38, and the DRAPartitionableDevices feature gate will then be locked on. To learn more, read Partitionable devices or refer to KEP-4815: DRA: Add support for partitionable devices. EvictionRequest API (alpha)Evicting a Pod isn’t always as simple as terminating it. Some applications may be in the middle of important work, such as data migration or cleanup, and terminating them without giving them time to prepare can cause disruptions. The EvictionRequest API introduces a more coordinated way to evict Pods. It gives applications and controllers time to prepare before a Pod is evicted. For example, when a node needs to be drained or a Pod needs to be moved to another node, a controller can create an EvictionRequest to signal that this Pod needs to be evicted. The eviction request controller coordinates with the responders configured for the Pod. These responders can perform application-specific tasks such as completing ongoing work, cleaning up resources, or migrating data before the Pod is terminated. If no custom responder is available or responders don't complete the process, Kubernetes can fall back to the existing API-initiated eviction mechanism, which continues to respect PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs). The EvictionRequest API does not replace PDBs. It gives applications a chance to participate in the eviction process. As this is an alpha feature, you will need to enable the EvictionRequestAPI feature gate and the relevant alpha API group. Check the v1.38 release notes and documentation, once they're available, to confirm exactly what's required. To learn more, refer to KEP-4563: EvictionRequest API. Want to know more?New features and deprecations are also announced in the Kubernetes release notes. We will formally announce what's new in Kubernetes v1.38 as part of the CHANGELOG for that release. title: [Kubernetes] Scheduling the removal of the kube-proxy IPVS backend
summary: The ipvs backend for kube-proxy was an experiment in providing a service proxy implementation with better performance than the iptables backend. While it succeeded in that goal, the kernel IPVS API has turned out to be a bad match for the Kubernetes Services API, and the ipvs backend was never able to implement all of the edge cases of Kubernetes Service functionality correctly. In Kubernetes 1.29, the project introduced the nftables backend for kube-proxy, which became GA in 1.33. Part of the plan behind adding the nftables backend was the idea that it would eventually replace both the iptables and ipvs backends. Because the ipvs backend in particular is complex, not 100% feature complete, and architecturally quite different from the other two backends (and thus more work to maintain), Kubernetes SIG Network decided to officially deprecate it as of Kubernetes 1.35. Although it currently remains available in kube-proxy (with a warning about its deprecation), we (Kubernetes SIG Network) now plan to remove it in Kubernetes 1.40. All ipvs users should therefore be planning to migrate to either the nftables or iptables backends. Why was the ipvs backend written?The ipvs backend was originally designed to fix two different kinds of performance problems in the iptables backend: First, iptables had problems with data plane latency (the speed at which clients could establish new connections to services), because kube-proxy would write a separate iptables rule to match each service IP, so every new connection would need to be matched against a long series of rules that was O(n) in the number of services in the cluster. Second, it had an even larger problem with control plane latency (the speed at which kube-proxy could process changes to services and endpoints and update the data plane rules), because kube-proxy would rewrite the entire iptables ruleset every time any service or endpoint changed. While the list of rules itself was only O(n) in the total number of endpoints, the amount of time, RAM, and CPU that it took to process the updated ruleset grew faster than that. In very large clusters, kube-proxy would use 100% of one CPU all the time just to process iptables updates. (In fact, the control plane scaling problem was bad enough that for most users it was not even possible to grow the cluster to the size where the data plane scaling problem became noticeable.) The ipvs backend solved both of these scaling problems. The data plane problem was solved mostly automatically, because the kernel IPVS subsystem uses hash tables rather than linear lookup. The control-plane problem was solved by not rewriting the entire ruleset on every update. (The kernel IPVS API doesn’t have a way of doing batch updates anyway, so this was essentially forced.) Why is the ipvs backend now being deprecated?Almost from the start, the ipvs backend also had problems. The first version didn’t have 100% compatibility with the iptables backend, but it was assumed that this would be fixed over time. Unfortunately, the original authors moved on to other things outside the Kubernetes ecosystem (as inevitably sometimes happens in open source), and it took a while to find new people interested in maintaining the code. Meanwhile, as people began using the ipvs backend in larger and larger clusters, its own scaling problems started to emerge. In particular, the lack of batch update operations in the IPVS API meant that while the ipvs backend was faster than iptables when making a few small changes, it was potentially slower when making a large number of changes at once. And because the IPVS API is fairly limited in what it can do, kube-proxy's ipvs backend needed to fall back to using iptables to implement various features of Kubernetes Services beyond basic "load balancing", making it run into some of the same scaling problems the iptables backend has. While the ipvs backend tried to mitigate this by using ipset for some of its rules, this again ran into the problem of not having a batch update API. Additionally, the fact that the ipvs backend uses iptables means that it has the same long-term support problem as the iptables backend: Red Hat's plan to remove the iptables API entirely from Red Hat Enterprise Linux means the ipvs kube-proxy backend will also no longer be available to Kubernetes users on RHEL. What about IPVS schedulers?Beyond performance, the other reason some users were excited about the ipvs backend was the ability to pick from among various IPVS "schedulers" for distributing traffic to endpoints, rather than relying on the simple random selection used by iptables (and nftables). Unfortunately, the way IPVS is used by kube-proxy prevents it from being able to use most of the IPVS schedulers in a useful way. The problem is that kube-proxy is a distributed service that runs on all nodes in the cluster, but the kube-proxy processes on different nodes do not share their IPVS scheduler state, so each node picks endpoints without knowing what is happening with clients on any other node. Even the schedulers that are designed to work in a distributed way generally don't work better than random selection in the context of kube-proxy. For example, the mh scheduler uses Maglev Hashing to select endpoints, which theoretically allows for extremely efficient distributed load balancing. But that efficiency is only in the context of a specific sort of two-layer load-balancer design, and kube-proxy does not have the right architecture to be able to act as either of the two layers in that design. Switching away from ipvsSwitching to nftablesIf you are running Kubernetes 1.36 or later, and your nodes are running a Linux distribution with kernel 5.13 or later, and you use the ipvs proxy mode, then Kubernetes recommends switching to the nftables mode of kube-proxy. (Although the nftables backend is GA —and fully usable—as of Kubernetes 1.33, there have been some performance- and scaling-related fixes since then that that weren't backported to releases earlier than 1.36.) The nftables backend is fully supported, feature-complete, and even has very slightly better performance than ipvs: (Taller bars represent longer latency. The "p50" group is the average connection establishment latency. Note that even the largest numbers in this graph are quite tiny; the point is not to claim that nftables is (noticeably) faster than ipvs, just to show that, unlike iptables, it's not slower.) Switching is as easy as changing the kube-proxy configuration and restarting kube-proxy. For example, in clusters deployed via kubeadm, change mode: ipvs to mode: nftables in the kube-proxy ConfigMap and then restart the kube-proxy pods, as described in the documentation on reconfiguring a kubeadm cluster. (If you are overriding other ipvs-specific kube-proxy configuration, you will also need to change those options to the corresponding nftables ones.) Switching to iptables: "It's Not As Slow As You Think!"If you can't switch to nftables, either because you are on an older version of Kubernetes, or because your cluster runs on an older Linux distribution that isn't new enough to support the nftables backend, you may be able to just switch to the iptables backend, which has improved greatly since the original creation of the ipvs backend in 2017: The generated ruleset has been optimized to remove redundant and irrelevant rules (#57461, #60306, #96959, #108251), reducing data plane latency. The code that generates the ruleset has been optimized to do fewer allocations, and to avoid unnecessarily recomputing the same information multiple times (#65755, #65902, #67948, #85617, #90103, #97238), reducing CPU and memory usage when resyncing. Rather than doing “check the current state of the rules, then update them to the new state”, iptables kube-proxy now does “assume the current state is correct, update to the new state based on that assumption, and only explicitly check the current state if that update fails”. This greatly improves the resyncing speed, because it turns out that even reading the iptables ruleset is extremely slow in large clusters (#81517, #110334, #114181). To the extent possible within the constraints of the iptables APIs, kube-proxy’s iptables backend now only updates iptables rules for services/endpoints that have changed since the last sync, rather than rewriting the entire ruleset every time (#110268 / KEP-3453). The net result of this is that the iptables backend of 2026, while still not as good as the ipvs backend, is at least much better than the iptables backend of 2017 was, and many people who found iptables unusable in the past would not have problems with it now. As with switching to nftables, switching to iptables is mostly just a matter of updating your kube-proxy configuration, although for technical reasons, in this case we recommend that you reboot each node after changing the kube-proxy configuration, rather than merely restarting kube-proxy. Learn more KEP-5495 gives the full timeline and plan for kube-proxy IPVS deprecation. The blog post "NFTables mode for kube-proxy" has more information about nftables mode and its performance relative to ipvs and iptables.

title: [Cloudflare] Probing DNS at Cloudflare
summary: Imagine this: you’ve just pushed a release. All the unit tests passed and your dashboards are green. You sit back to relax but then suddenly your phone starts blowing up: prod is broken.This is something the Cloudflare DNS team has experienced firsthand. In one rollout of the service that publishes DNS records to our edge, a scheduling bug let some record changes sit unpublished for hours. The service stayed up and was healthy, but new hostnames were slow to resolve and certificates couldn't be issued until the bug was squashed.DNS failures are hard to catch because they are slow, spread across the network, and partial in where they cause impact. We needed to figure out a way to test DNS the way customers experience it: constantly, from every data center, and against production.For us, the answer was to extend Flamingo, the end-to-end testing framework we were already using to run hundreds of millions of tests a day against Cloudflare's edge. This post covers how Flamingo's modular design lets us add DNS support, how we measure propagation, and how those measurements now decide whether a release goes ahead or gets rolled back.A little backgroundAt Cloudflare we’re obsessed with improving performance and safety for our customers. It’s crucial that our code is tested constantly, both at scale and against the real Cloudflare edge that our users operate in. That’s one reason why we created a tool called Flamingo: to measure the behavior of our production environments and make sure that code in lower-tier environments behaves as expected.We’ve already written a little about how this tool has been used in the upgrades to our CDN stack. However, this is only a small portion of how we use Flamingo internally. One of the features of Flamingo is its modular architecture that enables teams to extend the capabilities of the tool to speak other networking protocols. In our case, we wanted to use these modular capabilities to test DNS.What is Flamingo?Testing is hard. Testing at scale, when you have a widely distributed system, is even harder. There are many complex pathways that requests take and multiple systems that each network request must traverse before making its way to the origin. Unit testing alone is not nearly enough for this. We need to run constant automated testing against real systems and measure the outcomes of those requests to make informed decisions on the health of a service.Enter Flamingo. Originally built around complex multi-step HTTP testing, its capabilities and scope have increased substantially over the years. Flamingo is built from the ground up with Cloudflare’s infrastructure in mind. We built a control plane and scheduler that let teams target specific environments, data centers, or percentages of metals. We needed to integrate with custom reporting, metrics, and analytics tooling. Additionally, it needed to be a tool with predictable performance and run well on bare-metal servers in resource-constrained environments.Being delightfulWhen we’re building internal tooling like this, we strive to create a delightful developer experience. Internal tooling should be as easy as possible to use, but also powerful enough to handle over 80% of all use cases. And in order for a new edge acceptance test framework to be successful, it needs to be built in such a way that it forces teams to follow common guidelines and build reusable scripts in an environment that is stable, scalable, and manages complexity.One thing that is not delightful is debugging a test. If you allow a user to write tests in a traditional programming language, when their test fails they then both need to debug the upstream system being tested and the test itself. This is why we built Flamingo to use a custom domain-specific language (DSL) consisting of a simple setup-request-response format.For example, let’s imagine that we want to make sure we are redirecting all unencrypted traffic to its encrypted counterpart.TEST test-redirect SET $hostname www.cloudflare.com GET "http://$(hostname)/" ASSERT STATUS IS 301 ASSERT HEADER Location IS "https://$(hostname)/"Here we can see the power of the DSL. In five lines of code, we have a script that can run anywhere on Cloudflare’s edge and scale to thousands of requests per minute. We can take the data produced from the millions of data points generated from this and turn those into a graph defining how our service is actually performing in the real world.Taking the setup-request-response test format from above and modifying it slightly allows us to use Flamingo for more than just HTTP testing. Instead of the middle step being a request, we can now look at it as an action. Now we’ve changed our system from something that makes HTTP requests into something that can perform any action for which we’d like to measure the outcome.In Flamingo we call these modules and have put immense effort into making them as easy as possible for anyone to write. Flamingo is written in Rust, due to its consistent performance characteristics and strong type system. The type system in particular lends itself to this modularity, by allowing us to use strongly-typed enumerations for input and output in the Flamingo action runner:pub enum Action { Query { method: String, url: Expression, parameters: Vec<http::QueryParameters>, }, DnsQuery { query_name: Expression, query_type: Expression, parameters: Vec<dns::DnsQueryParameters>, }, } pub enum ActionOutput { Http(http::FetchResponse), Dns(dns::QueryResponse), } pub type ActionHandlerFunction = Arc< dyn Fn( Action, Arc<Ctx>, InterpreterConfig, ) -> BoxFuture<'static, Result<ActionOutput>> + Send + Sync + 'static, >; pub type ActionHandlerLUT = Arc< dyn Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction + Send + Sync + 'static, >;What we’ve done here is decouple the logic for performing an action (in this case an HTTP request) into a dynamically dispatched function that we can then call independently of other actions. This leaves things like test scheduling and resource management as higher-level operations that someone implementing a module doesn’t need to worry about. All the author needs to focus on is the logic.pub async fn query( action: Action, ctx: Arc<Ctx>, cfg: InterpreterConfig, ) -> Result<ActionOutput> { let Action::Query { method, url, parameters, } = action else { bail!("Invalid action for module-http::query: {action:?}"); }; ... } pub async fn execute_module<F>( ctx: Arc<Ctx>, cfg: &InterpreterConfig, handler_lut: F, ) -> Result<ActionOutput> where F: (Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction), { let func = handler_lut(action); let action_out = (func)(action.clone(), ctx.clone(), cfg.clone()).await?; ... }Using Flamingo to probe DNSThe adage says that when issues arise, it's always DNS. Like many jokes, there is always a kernel of truth behind it. DNS is an incredibly important piece of the Internet, and since it relies on a complex network of interconnected sources of truth, it can become easy for a single misstep to cause a storm of failures.DNS can be a particularly finicky system due to its hierarchical nature. When you change a DNS record for a Cloudflare zone, for example, said record needs to be propagated to the authoritative servers such that the updated record becomes widely available. To reduce latency, records are stored in physically closer caches. These records have a time to live (TTL) associated with them that tells the local DNS cache how long before it needs to refetch that record from the authoritative server. Any delays will impact time-sensitive operations like certificate issuance and traffic failover.We’ve already mentioned that we built Flamingo for extensibility. One of the first and most impactful modules in use today was built specifically for this use case. Our team was able to add code that extended Flamingo such that instead of sending HTTP requests, we send DNS queries. By doing so we got everything else for free. No need for the DNS team to worry about managing a new probing service. No need for them to have to integrate with our reporting pipelines. It all just worked.To probe DNS, we measure how quickly customer record changes propagate to authoritative nameservers and the public resolver (1.1.1.1). The test continuously updates a TXT record with a timestamp and queries three authoritative nameserver IPs and 1.1.1.1 from every data center, asserting freshness within 90s (authoritative) and 600s (resolver).TEST test-propagation-delay-direct-108-162-193-62 MOD dns SET $hostname "some.probe.domain" SET $authNs 108.162.193.62:53 # amir.ns.cloudflare.com QUERY $hostname TXT TARGET $authNs ASSERT DNS.RCODE IS NOERROR ASSERT DNS.FLAGS CONTAINS AA ASSERT DNS.ANSWERS GT SUBTRACT(TIMESTAMP(), "90")Catching bugs (SLO and steady)To ensure that our many systems are operating within expectations, we define what are called service-level objectives (SLOs) for observing things like availability or latency. SLOs are a percentage of some metric that is used as a target. Additionally, SLOs are measured through service-level indicators (SLIs) which are the actual series of measurements focused on the end-to-end experience that a user has when interacting with a system.By constantly sending synthetic Flamingo traffic through our production systems, we can begin to then use that information to build a picture of what our actual end users are experiencing — and provide that data for our SLOs. When that synthetic traffic encounters issues then we can be pretty confident that Cloudflare customers are also hitting issues and triage accordingly.Once we have this information, it allows us to make informed decisions when releasing a service. SLOs operate in terms of error budgets and burn rates. An error budget is the percentage of downtime that a service is willing to tolerate while the burn rate is the rate of change in that budget at any given time. This allows for an automated system to understand the severity of an issue. For example, burning 10% of your error budget over a three-day period might be some long running issue that, while not urgent, is affecting customers and needs to be dealt with. But if you were to burn 10% of your error budget within an hour, that means an incident is occurring and customer impact will be substantial if not fixed immediately.Using these numbers, we can look at our SLOs while deploying and make informed decisions on the health of a service. Based on that information, we can tell our releasing systems to either promote a change or roll it back.The road aheadBy moving DNS monitoring to Flamingo, we’ve created a system that can proactively detect DNS issues before they have the chance to spread to the rest of Cloudflare’s edge. If Flamingo detects a spike in propagation latency in a specific canary data center, we can automatically halt the rollout of a new software version before it impacts the rest of the Internet.DNS is just the start for extending Flamingo. We currently have modules for testing TCP, UDP, WebSockets, and several more. Having a tool for quickly testing and monitoring services has enabled teams to deploy large changes safely without the need for a human to keep a constant watch.If this kind of reliability engineering interests you, check out our careers page for open roles.

title: [Cloudflare] nginx2root: Five new nginx vulnerabilities, and how Cloudflare protects origins from the worst of them
summary: On November 18, 2026, F5 and nginx.org disclosed ten vulnerabilities in nginx. Five of them, detailed by the Xint research team and published under the name nginx2root, are memory corruption flaws that an unauthenticated attacker can use to crash an nginx worker or, per Xint's research, run commands on the server. Xint also found a Linux kernel bug that turns that foothold into root on the host, including from inside a Docker container. Other teams found the two HTTP/2 bugs independently: F5 also credits Rapid7, Wiz Research and Ikotas Labs for CVE-2026-123007, and Metnir, Wiz Research, and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for CVE-2026-123633.nginx is an HTTP web server that also serves as reverse proxy, content cache, load balancer, TCP/UDP proxy server, and mail proxy server. nginx runs a large share of the world's web servers, so this is a patch-now event. But if your nginx server is reachable only through Cloudflare's proxy, attackers cannot reach the vulnerable code paths for the most serious of these bugs, giving you protection while you update your servers.Here is where Cloudflare stands, what that protection covers, where it stops, and how the bugs work.The short versionCloudflare's edge is not affected. Much of the proxy that handles customer traffic at our edge now runs on FL2, written in Rust. We reviewed the parts still built on our heavily modified nginx fork against all five bugs before disclosure, and an update closing the related code paths finished rolling out globally before the vulnerabilities were published. The same releases fix five other nginx CVEs, including CVE-2026-118899, an infinite loop while reading a request body over TLS 1.3.Origins behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy are shielded from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks. For proxied hostnames, Cloudflare terminates every client HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connection at our edge and opens a separate connection to your origin. The attacker's frames never reach your nginx.The resolver and mail proxy vulnerabilities depend on specific configuration. Many configurations of nginx will not be vulnerable, but the safest way to be sure is to update your install or disable features.You should still patch. Update to nginx 1.30.7 or 1.31.9 (or your vendor's fixed build) and restart. Some configurations, covered below, are not protected by the proxy.What was disclosednginx2root is five independent bugs. Each one works on its own and each one needs a different configuration.CVEBug classAffected configurationFirst affected releaseCVE-2026-123007Integer overflow leading to out-of-bounds heap read/writeHTTP/2 enabled1.9.5 (2015)CVE-2026-123633Use-after-freeHTTP/2 with proxy_pass to a backend, worker low on worker_connections1.19.7CVE-2026-121810Use-after-freeHTTP/3 (QUIC) with proxy_pass to a backend1.25.0CVE-2026-123634Use-after-freeresolver + proxy_pass with variables + a subrequest (mirror or SSI)0.6.18CVE-2026-113425Use-after-freeMail proxy with proxy on and auth_http0.5.33F5 rates each one High (CVSS 3.1: 8.1) and Critical (CVSS 4.0: 9.2), and notes that code execution requires disabling or bypassing ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization). For CVE-2026-123007, Xint's write-up shows how it leaked memory addresses to do exactly that.CVE-2026-123007 is the one to worry about most. It only needs HTTP/2 turned on, which is commonly enabled on TLS deployments, and it has been in every nginx release since HTTP/2 support shipped in 1.9.5. Xint ran the exploit over the public Internet against servers on AWS, GCP and Azure. Xint searched Shodan on November 10, before the disclosure, and found 56.7 million hosts matching product:nginx. Of the 11.94 million that reported a version, 98.9% fell in the affected range. As of November 19, Censys's nginx2root exposure tracker counts about 8.8 million services running a potentially affected version with HTTP/2 enabled. Version strings don't prove a host is vulnerable, since distributions backport fixes, but the exposure is large.The same nginx releases also fix five other bugs. The most serious, CVE-2026-118899, is an infinite loop when reading a request body over TLS 1.3 that lets an unauthenticated attacker stall a worker, in nginx 1.13.0 and later.The Linux kernel bug is the sixth part of nginx2root. Xint found a use-after-free in the kernel's SCTP send path, present since Linux 4.15 (2018): while a send operation waits, its SCTP association can be moved to another socket, and the waiting send can then free it. An attacker who already runs code as the nginx worker can use it to gain root on the host, and Xint did this from an nginx running inside a Docker container. Many distributions load the SCTP module automatically the first time a program opens an SCTP socket, so hosts that never use SCTP can still be exposed. As of November 18, no kernel fix was available and Xint was withholding the details until there is one.As of November 19, none of the five nginx2root CVEs is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and we have not seen reports of exploitation in the wild. Xint and Wiz Research have not released their exploits. Rapid7 has published a proof of concept, which it describes as suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started local container. Fake 'exploits' are also circulating on GitHub.Why Cloudflare's proxy protects your originnginx2root's most dangerous bugs live in how nginx parses and manages HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connections. To trigger them, an attacker has to send a carefully ordered stream of protocol frames directly to the nginx process: billions of WINDOW_UPDATE frames, a SETTINGS frame that holds response data back, PING frames that fill the send buffers, partial HEADERS frames, RST_STREAM at exactly the right moment.When your DNS record is proxied through Cloudflare, that connection ends at our edge.Cloudflare reads the client's HTTP request, applies your security and caching rules, and then makes its own request to your origin over a connection Cloudflare controls. The flow-control frames, pings, settings, and stream resets that the attacker sends are consumed by our edge. They are not forwarded. Your nginx only ever sees the requests Cloudflare chooses to send, framed the way Cloudflare frames them. This also holds when Cloudflare connects to your origin over HTTP/2: Cloudflare runs its own flow control on that connection and sends WINDOW_UPDATE and RST_STREAM frames only as its own traffic needs, so a client can't make it relay the billions of WINDOW_UPDATE frames the attack requires.Rapid7 makes the same point in its analysis of CVE-2026-123007: if the HTTP/2 connection is proxied, the attacker's frames "will likely not be retransmitted" in a way that allows exploitation. This breaks each of the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks.CVEWhat the attacker needsBehind Cloudflare's HTTP proxyCVE-2026-123007Direct control over HTTP/2 WINDOW_UPDATE, SETTINGS, PING and RST_STREAM on one connection to nginxProtected. Control frames terminate at Cloudflare's edge.CVE-2026-123633The first part of a HEADERS frame on a direct HTTP/2 connection, plus the ability to exhaust nginx connection slots and reset the TCP connectionProtected. The client's HTTP/2 connection terminates at Cloudflare.CVE-2026-121810A direct QUIC/HTTP/3 connection to nginxProtected. HTTP/3 terminates at Cloudflare's edge. We do not communicate to origins over HTTP/3CVE-2026-123634A request and its mirror or SSI subrequest waiting on the same DNS lookup, and the main request ending while the answer is processed. In Xint's exploit, nginx's resolver had to reach the attacker's DNS server.Not fully protected. Depends on how your config builds proxy_pass. Patch.CVE-2026-113425A direct IMAP/POP3/SMTP connection to the nginx mail proxyNot protected. Cloudflare's HTTP proxy does not carry mail traffic.There is one condition to be protected by Cloudflare here: your origin must not be reachable directly. If an attacker can find your origin's IP and connect to it directly (TCP 443 or 80 for HTTP/2, UDP 443 for HTTP/3, or the mail ports), Cloudflare isn't in the path and the protection doesn't apply. You should ensure that your origin servers can only be accessed through Cloudflare’s proxies, using one of the following approaches:Cloudflare Tunnel. Your origin makes an outbound-only connection to Cloudflare and exposes no inbound ports.Firewall to Cloudflare IP ranges. Accept inbound HTTP/HTTPS only from Cloudflare's published IP ranges. This must be done using an IP firewall, not based on configuration in your nginx server.Authenticated Origin Pulls (mTLS). Your origin rejects any TLS connection that doesn't present Cloudflare's client certificate.Xint's own exposure check makes the same point: "If a CDN or reverse proxy sits in front of nginx, the test only reaches the proxy, so also run it directly against the nginx server."Where the protection does not applyThere are several situations in which Cloudflare’s HTTP proxy does not provide protection.Spectrum TCP/UDP applications. For these configurations, traffic from the Internet is passed unmodified through to your origin. If your origin is running nginx, patch or disable the affected features.nginx mail proxy. Cloudflare's HTTP proxy does not carry IMAP, POP3 or SMTP. Restrict mail listeners to trusted networks until patched.CVE-2026-123634 (resolver). This depends on how your configuration builds the proxy_pass target from the request, combined with a carefully timed cancellation of an HTTP request. Passing your traffic through Cloudflare’s proxy makes it harder to exploit this, but does not provide full protection. Update regardless.DNS-only (grey-cloud), internal or non-proxied nginx. Any nginx server an attacker can reach without going through Cloudflare, including internal services behind a compromised host, needs to be patched.Cloudflare’s WAF rules are not relevant to these vulnerabilities. These are protocol-level bugs. Because Cloudflare’s proxy handles parsing the HTTP protocol messages, and creates new messages to fetch information from origin servers, origins behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy are protected from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 bugs without needing a rule. We have therefore not released a managed rule. The protection comes from connection termination, not from pattern matching.What to do nowFind every nginx server. Include nginx Plus, distribution packages, container images and appliances. Run nginx -V and nginx -T on each and note HTTP/2, HTTP/3/QUIC listeners, proxy_pass with variables plus SSI or mirror, and any mail block.Patch. Update nginx Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, nginx Plus to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1, or your distribution's fixed package. F5 lists nginx Plus R34 to R36 as affected with no fixed build, so move those to a fixed 37.x release. Then restart nginx or complete a binary upgrade. A config reload does not replace the running binary.Check backport versions carefully. Distributions often patch without changing the version nginx -v reports. Compare the full package version against your distribution's advisory.Make sure your origin is only reachable through Cloudflare. Use Tunnel, IP allowlisting or Authenticated Origin Pulls.If you can't patch yet, disable what you don't need. http2 off; (nginx 1.25.1 and later; on older versions, remove http2 from the listen directive) blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. Removing QUIC listeners and setting http3 off; blocks CVE-2026-121810. Point proxy_pass at fixed upstream groups for CVE-2026-123634. Don't rely on mirror_request_body alone: Xint's tested setup set it to off, and the default on stopped that exploit, but SSI and other subrequests can still reach the bug. Bind mail listeners to trusted networks for CVE-2026-113425. Restart so old connections close.Block SCTP if you don't use it. Add install sctp /bin/false to a file in /etc/modprobe.d/ to stop the kernel module from loading. This doesn't unload an already-loaded module or disable SCTP built into the kernel. When your distribution ships a kernel update for the SCTP bug, install it and reboot. Blocking the module is a stopgap until then.The Cloudflare Radar Zero Wire entry for nginx2root has the full checklist, a prompt you can give an agent to run a read-only assessment of your fleet, and links to every vendor advisory.Technical deep diveLet’s dig into the details of the five bugs by looking through the code. We’re looking at nginx 1.31.8 (commit 140aa94) which was the most recent code published before the fixes, and comparing this to the fixes in 1.31.9 (which were also included in release 1.30.7 on the stable branch).A note on methodology: we based our analysis on the public advisories, and to verify our reading of the code, we built the public 1.31.8 and 1.31.9 releases with AddressSanitizer and ran tests for four of the five bugs (flow control, HTTP/2 use-after-free, resolver and mail proxy). Each one faults on 1.31.8 and runs clean on 1.31.9. We did not reproduce the HTTP/3 bug; that section is based on the fix commit and the published analysis.One pattern, in four placesFour of the five bugs are use-after-free bugs. This is a common issue with programs that manually manage memory without language support: one part of the code frees an object that another part is still using.nginx is event driven. A handler runs, calls other code, and that code returns to the handler. Three of the bugs occur when the called code tears down the connection or request the handler is working on. In the fourth, a second connection still holds a pointer to the object.CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-121810. A request needs a connection slot to reach its upstream. nginx is low on slots, so it closes an idle connection to free one. The connection it chooses is the one the request belongs to.CVE-2026-123634. A resolver callback ends a request. Cleanup of that request frees a second resolver context that the resolver is about to call next.CVE-2026-113425. When a write to a mail client fails, the client connection is closed while the connection to the authentication service still points at its session.F5 rates all four as potential code execution if address space layout randomization (ASLR) is disabled or bypassed, and in its tests Xint reports code execution with the privileges of the nginx worker.The fifth bug, CVE-2026-123007, is of a different kind: an accounting error that becomes a length error. CVE-2026-123007: two flow-control pieces that each look correctHTTP/2 flow control limits the amount of response data a server may send. nginx tracks a send window for each stream and one for the connection, h2c->send_window. The client enlarges a window with a WINDOW_UPDATE frame, and the protocol caps every window at 2^31 − 1.nginx enforces that cap when a WINDOW_UPDATE arrives (ngx_http_v2_state_window_update()):if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) { /* logs "client violated connection flow control" */ return ngx_http_v2_connection_error(h2c, NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR); }On its own, this check is correct. But the connection window also grows in a second place. When nginx queues DATA frames for a stream, it subtracts their length from the window. If the stream is canceled before those frames go out, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() takes them off the queue and returns the credit:h2c->send_window += window;Nothing caps this line. As the fix commit describes, if the client enlarges the connection window after the frames are queued and before the stream is terminated, the refund pushes the window past 2^31 − 1.From that point the first check no longer works. h2c->send_window is an unsigned size_t, so NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window wraps around to a very large number and every subsequent WINDOW_UPDATE is accepted. The client can then raise the window as far as it wants.The window is unsigned, but the code that sizes DATA frames compares it as a signed value (ngx_http_v2_send_chain()):if (limit == 0 || limit > (off_t) h2c->send_window) { limit = h2c->send_window; } ... if ((off_t) frame_size > limit) { frame_size = (size_t) limit; }After the window passes 2^63, it is negative as an off_t. The frame size becomes the window value itself, a number between 2^63 and 2^64, and nginx builds a buffer whose last pointer lies before its pos pointer.Over TLS, that buffer reaches a memcpy() in ngx_ssl_send_chain() with that length. Our TLS test stops at that point under AddressSanitizer. Xint's write-up explains how, with the window pushed close to 2^64, this turns into a controlled out-of-bounds write and an address leak, and Xint, Rapid7, and Wiz each report code execution from it. This post goes no further than the fault.Over cleartext HTTP/2, the same invalid buffer follows a different output path. Our cleartext test also faults under AddressSanitizer on 1.31.8 and runs clean on 1.31.9. The public write-ups address the TLS case.How much traffic the known attacks requireThe biggest step a WINDOW_UPDATE can take is 2^31 − 1, and a WINDOW_UPDATE frame is 13 bytes. Bringing a 64-bit window near its top therefore requires about 2^33 frames: roughly 8.6 billion frames, or about 112 GB (104 GiB).Rapid7, which published a proof of concept, gives the same figure and adds that nginx limits control-frame traffic relative to other traffic on the connection, so its run also sends about 15 GiB of other request traffic. Its total comes to approximately 128 GB of HTTP/2 data: about two minutes on a 10 Gbit/s link and about seventeen minutes at 1 Gbit/s. Rapid7 estimates the WINDOW_UPDATE traffic needed to reach 2^63 at about 2^32 frames, or 52 GiB, half of the 104 GiB figure. It also notes that these figures describe its route and are not a proven minimum.For defenders, this is the useful fact about the bug. At this volume, the known attacks are hard to hide: nginx receives tens of gigabytes from a single client over one long-lived connection and sends little back, much more than the requests in the access log account for.Why it was difficult to findThe refund line has existed in nginx since HTTP/2 support arrived in 1.9.5 in 2015. Two things made it difficult to notice.First, each piece looks correct on its own. The check on WINDOW_UPDATE is the right check. The refund is the right refund. The bug is that the check relies on an assumption the refund does not preserve.Second, testing that waits for a crash is very unlikely to reach it, because a crash requires tens of gigabytes of input. The bad state itself can be reached with very little traffic: Censys published a cleartext test that reaches what it calls the corrupted flow-control state with a 5.69 MB capture. A test that asserts "the send window never exceeds its protocol maximum" after every frame would flag the bad state as soon as a test sequence got there. A test that waits for memory corruption would not.The fixThe fix (6 lines added) introduces a counter, h2c->send_queued, for DATA that is queued but not yet sent. The WINDOW_UPDATE check now includes those bytes in the window:if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window - h2c->send_queued) {From the client's perspective, queued frames still count toward the window, so the client can no longer refill credit that nginx is about to refund. On a fixed version the attempt is rejected with a flow-control error.CVE-2026-123633: where two protections interactAn nginx worker has a fixed number of connection slots (worker_connections), which the client and upstream connections share. Since 1.19.2, when free slots run low (1/16 of the total or fewer), ngx_get_connection() calls ngx_drain_connections(), which closes connections marked "reusable": connections with nothing in progress, such as idle keep-alive connections.This works only if a reusable connection truly has nothing in progress. For HTTP/2 that was not always the case. Two commits landed on the same day in February 2021 and were released together in 1.19.7:"HTTP/2: fixed reusing connections with active requests" fixed a case in which a cleartext HTTP/2 connection could remain reusable while it had a request."HTTP/2: reuse of connections with incomplete frames" registered a connection as reusable while it waits for the remainder of a partly received frame, so that a client cannot hold slots with partial frames.The second change is the relevant one here.
