title: [Pulumi] How FIPS led to leaner container images for everyone
summary: It started with a familiar story. A Trivy scan of our service image flagged six distinct critical vulnerabilities and nine distinct high-severity vulnerabilities across curl and libcurl. We expected to rush out a patch. Then we traced what curl was doing in the image. Its only job was to make a health check request to localhost. Did we need it there at all? That question took on more urgency as we worked with teams running self-hosted Pulumi Cloud in air-gapped networks or inside FedRAMP authorization boundaries. When those teams run our images inside their own networks, every package in them becomes theirs to scan, justify in a security review, and keep patched. Anything we ship that doesn’t need to be there becomes their problem, too. Today, four new FIPS image variants are generally available on Docker Hub — three for self-hosted Pulumi Cloud, and one for customer-managed runners. The changes we’ve made apply to our standard container images too, so everyone running self-hosted Pulumi Cloud or customer-managed runners now gets leaner images, whether or not they need FIPS. Here’s how we got there. Charting a course to FIPS mode for each image FIPS, short for Federal Information Processing Standards, is the U.S. government’s set of rules for cryptography. For a FIPS image, the first thing that matters is where its cryptography comes from. The FIPS images for self-hosted Pulumi Cloud cover three pieces: the API service, the console (the web app), and a small tool that applies database migrations. The API service and the migrations tool are Go programs, and Go brings its own cryptographic module, so we could run those two in FIPS mode, where they use only FIPS-approved cryptography. The console, a Node.js app, was a different story, so we started with the API and came back to it. Replacing curl with a single-purpose binary We traced curl in the API and workflow pool images back to their container health checks. While looking for a way to remove it, we realized we’d already built a similar probe for local development. We extended it into http_health, a small binary that only sends requests to loopback addresses. The container health checks, API integration tests, and local dependency checks now use the same probe. Our API tests already used their own certificate authority (CA), so we made custom CA support part of the probe. Removing curl cleared those findings from the API image. The migrations image turned out to be a freebie. It runs a small Go program to apply database migrations, and there was nothing extra we needed to strip out. Both binaries carried Go’s cryptographic module, so we could enable FIPS mode and keep Alpine, at least for now. Two images down. Then came the console. Rewriting the console backend in Go The curl work left us with a question for the FIPS console build: what does this image actually need at runtime, and what is just along for the ride? The console had run on Alpine for years, most recently on the standard Node.js 22 Alpine image. A small Express backend handled sign-in and configuration and served the Angular frontend. The Node.js console leans on OpenSSL, so it needed a base image with OpenSSL’s FIPS provider, the component that supplies FIPS-approved cryptography, and a host running in FIPS mode. We started with Red Hat Universal Base Image (UBI) 9. Getting the console running in FIPS mode on UBI 9 was a milestone. We had a working image with the same backend and frontend. Once the honeymoon was over, we had to reckon with what came along for the ride. UBI brought a lot more operating system than our Alpine image, and the scans showed it. The image meant for teams with the strictest security requirements carried more CVEs than our standard one, and keeping both patched meant maintaining two different foundations. It was clear we still had some work to do before this felt right. We could start with a smaller UBI image, strip out what we didn’t need, and harden what remained. That would trim the image, but the console would still depend on Node.js and OpenSSL. For a backend that mostly handled sign-in and served an Angular app, it was worth asking whether we needed Node.js at runtime at all. We decided to rewrite the backend in Go. We called it “Node to Go.” There was a little gratitude in that name for the Node.js backend we were saying goodbye to, and no mystery about where we were headed. It was also close enough to Chappell Roan’s “HOT TO GO!” to give the rewrite a soundtrack. Then came the first test scan of the rebuild. We built both FIPS console images within a minute of each other and scanned them with the same version of Trivy. We expected fewer findings. Seeing the scan findings drop from 249 to two was still striking. Releasing agent containers and binaries together The customer-managed workflow agent is the one image in this release that some customers build themselves. We publish a container and a standalone binary for teams that want to package it their own way. The agent uses semantic versions, like our open-source tools, and has its own release cadence. A version like v2.3.4 should mean the same thing however you get it. Adding the FIPS image gave us a reason to revisit how we shipped both. The public agent repo depended on private service code, which made it harder for people outside Pulumi to clone the repo and contribute. We moved the build and signing into our release pipeline. The public repository now verifies the signed files from get.pulumi.com and mirrors them to GitHub Releases. Existing download links still work, and a base-image or Go dependency update can go out as an agent patch without someone having to cut a release by hand. Putting scan results in charge of releases We came out of this with less software in the images and a simpler release process. The next job was keeping those images lean and patched. We kept the tools you’ll see across our open-source repos: Dependabot alerts flag vulnerable dependencies, and Renovate opens pull requests with updates. We adopted Grype after comparing our scan results with what customers were seeing, and moved image scans earlier in the release process so we could catch problems before publication. The change was putting those scan results in charge of whether an image ships. When a fix becomes available for a serious vulnerability, the clock starts. If the image still contains the vulnerability after our remediation window, the pipeline blocks publication and alerts our team. The same check applies to standard and FIPS images, so every self-hosted Pulumi Cloud customer gets images held to the same patching policy. Moving to a distroless base Getting the console back onto Alpine showed how much we could strip away and still run the same application. With the API, console, and migrations all running as statically compiled Go binaries, we decided to see how much of Alpine we still needed. We had to revisit what our code assumed about the environment it ran in, from where it got time zone data to whether the images started on both CPU architectures we support. We made the runtime dependencies explicit and tested the images on both architectures. That let us move the API, console, and migrations to a distroless base without a shell or package manager. What ships today If you run Pull from Docker Hub Self-hosted Pulumi Cloud pulumi/service-fips, pulumi/console-fips, and pulumi/migrations-fips Customer-managed runners pulumi/customer-managed-workflow-agent-fips Helping customers run Pulumi in environments that require FIPS made us more demanding about what we ship to everyone who runs our images. Every dependency in an image you run yourself is something we have to maintain and something a customer might have to explain in a security review. We want to give you fewer of those to account for and get fixes into your hands sooner. That’s the standard we’ll keep pushing for across our images.

title: [Pulumi] Least privilege by default: what's new in Pulumi Cloud RBAC
summary: Access control in Pulumi Cloud now starts from least privilege. Every organization gets three new built-in roles, you can share a single stack or environment with a teammate, and you can create service principals to give your automated workloads their own identity. Why change how access works? Protecting your infrastructure is central to how we build Pulumi Cloud, and access control has to keep up with how teams work. More people outside the platform team touch infrastructure, and a growing share of changes comes from pipelines and coding agents, which need to be governed as carefully as the people they work for. Security works best when the secure choice is also the convenient one. Giving people, agents, and automation the access they need, and nothing more, shouldn’t take extra work. The changes below make the narrow, deliberate choice the default one. Three new built-in roles Every organization now has three new built-in roles, alongside Admin and Billing Manager. Each one includes everything the one before it allows: Role What members can do Reader See the organization’s stacks, environments, and cloud accounts. Builder Everything a Reader can, plus create stacks, environments, and cloud accounts, and manage the ones they create. Maintainer Everything a Builder can, plus change every stack, environment, and cloud account in the organization. One of them is the organization’s default role, the role members have unless an admin assigns them a different one. New organizations start on Builder: people create and manage their own infrastructure, and get access to everyone else’s when someone decides they should. Existing organizations were moved to a built-in role that matches what their members could already do, or kept their existing default, so nobody gained or lost access. When an admin changes the default role, every member who follows it moves to the new role, and members who were assigned a role keep theirs. Share one stack with one person Giving one person access to one thing now takes a few seconds. Every stack, environment, and cloud account has Access settings: select Add Principal, pick a teammate, pick what they can do, and you’re done. Teams are granted access in the same place, so a single list shows everyone who has been granted access to that stack, environment, or cloud account. Every organization also has an Everyone team that always contains every member, for the things the whole organization should see. Service principals: an identity for automation A service principal is an identity for work that isn’t done by a person. You create it, name it, and give it access the same way you would a teammate: It starts with nothing. A service principal doesn’t follow the organization’s default role. It has only the roles and access you give it, so it can be as narrow as a single stack and the environments that stack imports. You grant access where you already do. Add a service principal from the same Access settings you use to share a stack, environment, or cloud account with a teammate, or assign it a role for the whole organization. It can’t be used to get around your own access. Admins, Maintainers, and Builders can create service principals, and can only give one the roles they could grant themselves. It shows up by name. In the audit logs, a service principal is the actor of everything it does, so you can tell which automation made a change. Pulumi Cloud also creates service principals where it runs work for you: each Pulumi Delivery pipeline that doesn’t name its own identity and each custom agent gets one of its own. Pipelines run as who you choose We recently introduced Pulumi Delivery, which lets you write your release pipeline as a Pulumi program. Every Delivery pipeline runs as one identity. The person who starts a run, approves a gate, or pushes a commit doesn’t lend the run their own access. By default, Delivery generates a service principal for each pipeline and gives it access to the stacks the pipeline works with and nothing else. To decide the access yourself, name a service principal you created, or a team, in the pipeline program: const pipeline = new delivery.Pipeline("shop", { servicePrincipal: { userId: "service-principal:0b6f1c2e-5d3a-4f7b-9c1d-2e8a7b6c5d4f" }, }); flowchart LR A --> R B --> R R -->|runs as| SP SP --> S SP --> E Runs are predictable. A run that works when you start it also works when a push starts it overnight, because it’s the same identity both times. The access is yours to decide. The pipeline can reach what its service principal was given and nothing else. It’s visible. The pipeline’s settings list the service principals and teams it has been registered with, and who added each one. Pulumi Deployments works the same way. A stack’s deployment settings now have a Run as setting: select a service principal, or a team, and every deployment of that stack runs with that identity’s access, whether it’s started by a person, a git push, or a schedule. Restricted by default for new organizations New organizations are created in the restricted permission mode, where automation gets only the access you explicitly gave it. Every stack’s deployments run as a service principal or a team, and a team access token gets its team’s access and nothing more. Existing organizations keep working the way they always have, with automation that can get broader access than you gave it, until an admin switches them to restricted. The console spells out what the switch changes before you confirm. Manage it as code If you manage your organization with the Pulumi Service provider, version 1.7.0 covers the new model: you can set the default role, assign the built-in roles, and give a member access to a single stack, environment, or cloud account: resources: aliceOnDev: type: pulumiservice:OrganizationMemberEntityAccess properties: organizationName: my-org username: alice entityType: stack entityName: my-project/dev permission: stack-write What changes for existing organizations? Nothing changes until you choose to change it. Your members kept their access when the built-in roles arrived, your custom roles and teams work as before, and your deployments keep running the way they do today. To move an existing organization to least privilege, take these steps in order: Pick a default role. For most organizations, that’s Builder. Give each stack that uses Pulumi Deployments a service principal or a team with access to what that stack needs. Switch to the restricted permission mode once each of those stacks has one. The permission modes documentation has a short checklist, and you can switch back if something was missed. Next steps Everything here is available today. The documentation notes where a feature depends on your edition. Read how default roles and access on individual stacks work. Create a service principal, then name it in a Delivery pipeline or select it under Run as in a stack’s deployment settings. Share feedback in the Pulumi Community Slack or on GitHub.

title: [Netflix] Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System
summary: By Shreya S Ramanujam, Yongce Li, Afshine Amidi, Sina Ghiassian, Benjamin Klein.IntroductionPicture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen:If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. We see two types of synopses here: a series-level synopsis describing the overarching plot, and multiple episode-level synopses describing each episode.A synopsis plays a very important role for us — it helps viewers decide whether a title is worth watching or not. Every synopsis needs to strike a balance: sharing just enough to give viewers a sense of what to expect, while leaving enough intrigue to draw them in. But of course, we can’t just write anything.“In the fog-drenched streets of Victorian London, Detective Daphne Bridgerton races to unmask a serial killer known only as the elusive Lady Whistledown.”Intriguing? Definitely. But it is most certainly not the premise of Bridgerton. Which leads us to the first (and most important) rule of writing a good synopsis: it must be factual. At Netflix’s scale, with thousands of titles, multiple episodes per season and multiple languages, fact-checking all of these by hand simply doesn’t scale. This is where our factuality service comes in: an automated way to judge whether a synopsis is factual or not.Our current factuality checker feeds a reasoning model everything we know about a title (like metadata and text assets) and asks it to judge synopsis factuality according to a rigorous rubric. There are two main limitations of this approach that we want to optimize:High cost of long-context reasoning calls: Each decision requires expensive, long-context model calls to reasoning models, which doesn’t scale well when we want to check multiple titles, episodes, languages, and style variants.Misaligned rationales: The model’s explanations often diverge from our annotators’ reasoning, which makes its factuality verdicts less reliable. We want these rationales to be better aligned so that (1) the model can consistently flag nuanced errors, and (2) its explanations can be used downstream to automatically correct issues in the synopsis.Our new approach tackles both problems at once. On the cost side, it delivers a 52.4% reduction per synopsis. On the quality side, it significantly improves both verdict accuracy and reasoning alignment: Recall–Fail (“Of all truly non-factual synopses, how many does the system correctly reject?”) rises from 0.77 to 0.86, and the new factuality service’s explanations now show ~82% overlap with human rationales (up from ~69%). In other words, it’s not just cheaper and more accurate — it’s also much better aligned with how our expert annotators actually judge synopses.So, what exactly does factuality mean?Let’s go back to the Bridgerton example. Say you see this synopsis about Bridgerton Season 1:Synopsis A: “Bridgerton follows Daphne Bridgerton, the eldest daughter of the powerful Bridgerton family as she makes her debut onto Regency London’s competitive marriage market.”It’s easy to judge that this synopsis is factually correct — no wrong facts, and it gives the reader a clear, accurate glimpse of what to expect from the show.Let’s take another example:Synopsis B: “Set in modern-day London, this gritty crime drama follows Detective Daphne Bridgerton as she hunts a serial killer while hiding her own criminal past.”Another easy one — the plot is so blatantly off the mark that it is definitely not factual.But what about this?Synopsis C: “Bridgerton follows the mysterious, sharp-tongued Lady Whistledown as she exposes the secrets of London’s high society through her scandalous gossip sheet.”Technically, every statement here is true — Lady Whistledown does indeed publish a gossip sheet, and if there’s one thing she is known for, it’s her scathing exposés. So then, is this a factual synopsis?Not quite! While technically true, it paints a misleading picture of the show. A new viewer might reasonably expect it to revolve around Lady Whistledown, rather than Daphne navigating the marriage market. This, too, is a type of non-factuality we want to catch.Lastly, here’s the trickiest of all:Synopsis D: “When Daphne Bridgerton makes her society debut, she catches the eye of the aloof Duke of Hastings, and the two begin a passionate love affair that sets the whole ton abuzz.”Again, every statement is true, but the phrasing is misleading. A new viewer might assume they fall in love immediately, missing the fact that their relationship begins as a fake, mutually beneficial arrangement. This is another type of nuanced error our system should flag.So now that we have an idea of the kinds of errors we care about, the real question is: how do we build a system that is able to catch both glaring as well as subtle factuality violations?Current Service and Its LimitationsOur current factuality pipeline is a straightforward, holistic LLM call. We feed a reasoning model everything we know about a title (text assets, metadata, and a detailed factuality rubric) and ask it to judge the factuality of a synopsis. We repeat the call several times to reduce output randomness, and if any run flags the synopsis as non-factual, it fails. This approach has two main limitations:High cost: Each judgment requires multiple (five, to be exact) calls to a large reasoning model over extremely long contexts (100k+ tokens), which does not scale well.Misaligned reasoning: The model can fail synopses for nitpicky reasons (e.g., “This is a show about wonderful magic” gets failed because the characters never literally call the magic “wonderful”) while overlooking nuanced errors by convincing itself they “don’t really make the synopsis false.” This misalignment makes verdicts less reliable and rationales less useful for downstream correction.Optimizing the Holistic PipelineTo understand exactly where we should optimize the current holistic pipeline, we study the current pipeline both qualitatively and quantitatively on a custom factuality benchmark that we built. This benchmark comprises synopses hand-labeled by human annotators as factual or non-factual, along with their rationales. This analysis reveals several key insights:Insight 1: Do we really need five holistic calls?Let’s think back to why we added multiple holistic calls in the first place: to reduce sampling noise. In practice, though, we see an interesting dichotomy:Blatantly true / false synopses (Bridgerton A, B): All runs agree on the verdict with near-identical reasoning.Nuanced errors (Bridgerton C, D): The model is much more likely to disagree with itself — some runs catch the error, some don’t. This is exactly where additional sampling helps.This suggests a simple optimization: A and B don’t really need all 5 calls. If we can somehow identify these “easy” synopses upfront, we can cut down on the number of calls for them, while still giving harder cases like C and D the extra calls they need.The easiest way to do this is to ask the model to output its confidence alongside its verdict and rationale. We can then separate “easy” (high confidence) synopses from “hard” (low confidence) ones and only send the hard cases through additional checks. Think of it like airport security: most bags go straight through, but those that trigger the alarm (low confidence) get extra screening.Implementing this easy fix makes our pipeline go from the current holistic model to a new “confidence gated” holistic model:Insight 2: Five identical judges calls give us no new informationWith confidence gating, our pipeline only escalates harder synopses to the full five holistic calls. But extra calls only help with sampling noise, not systematic reasoning errors: if every run follows the same flawed rationale, they’ll all reach the same wrong verdict, rendering the extra calls useless. How can we ensure that each call counts?Idea: Diversify the judges and make them specializedInstead of running five holistic judges with the same generic factuality prompt, we introduce two specialized judges that individually target the two aspects of factuality we care about:Literal Judge: Is the synopsis literally true?Implicature Judge: Does this synopsis give a false picture to a new reader who has not watched this show?Explicitly searching for specific types of errors helps us better flag both literal and subtler implicature errors. In practice, we observe that this works better than repeatedly querying a single holistic judge, hoping that sampling stochasticity will surface nuanced errors.Insight 3: The rationale reveals mistakes the verdict hidAt this point, we have a pretty good pipeline, but we’re still underusing one of the richest signals available to us: the model’s rationale behind its verdict. For nuanced errors, we often see the model identify a point of contention, then brush it aside based on a faulty assumption or because it deems the issue too minor to affect the verdict. Can we use these shaky spots in the rationale to catch (and correct) errors the verdict misses?Idea: Secondary atomic-claim checking via a router:Since our literal and implicature judges are already strong reasoning models, we ask them to additionally critically analyse their own reasoning and surface shaky spots — any doubts, concessions, or assumptions that might need rechecking. These include cases where the model:Makes an assumption.Raises a doubt that the available evidence can’t resolve (e.g., an external critic quote).Notices a contradiction but dismisses it as insufficient to change the verdict.We pass all concessions from both judges to a router model, which:Reframes them as self-contained, verifiable atomic claims, each with a materiality field specifying the evidence needed to support or refute it.Routes each claim to the appropriate secondary Stage-2 judge: a web judge for external facts (e.g., citations, media quotes, or prior work), or a source-material recheck focused on the reframed atomic claim. By pinpointing the exact point of contention, the recheck is more targeted, making it easier to mark the claim as true or false.Putting It All Together: Proposed Cascade Factuality ServiceOur findings lead to three key improvements: specialized judges, confidence-gated escalation, and targeted rechecking of shaky reasoning using a secondary stage when escalated.We implement these improvements as a tiered system shown in the figure below: every synopsis first passes through both the literal and the implicature judges. High-confidence verdicts are retained, while low-confidence cases escalate to the router and Stage-2 judges for further checking. Stage 2 can overturn the initial verdict in two cases:FAIL → PASS: All concessions, including the original failure reasons, are supported by the secondary check.PASS → FAIL: At least one concession is contradicted.ResultsBased on our discussions from above, we evaluate three different pipelines:Evaluation: Datasets and MetricsWe evaluate these systems on two datasets: show-level and episode-level synopses. Each datapoint includes a synopsis, a human gold label (factual / not factual), and the annotator’s rationale. For episode-level synopses, we additionally require that the synopsis be specific to that particular episode, not just a generic synopsis of the overall show.We focus on two main axes: Quality and Cost. The quality metrics are listed below:Recall-FAIL is our primary metric: higher recall means fewer Gold FAILs are missed. We also track Precision-PASS, which measures how reliably PASS verdicts identify Gold PASSes, and alignment with human rationales.On the cost side, we want to reduce both the average number of LLM calls per synopsis and the end-to-end cost of producing a final verdict. Latency is not our primary optimization target, but we do want to ensure the median (P50) latency does not blow up to impractical judgement times.Evaluation ResultsThe best numbers per metric per dataset are shown in bold.Note: We compared the cascade against two holistic ablations — increased reasoning effort and a smaller, cheaper model — to test if simple ablations could achieve better performance. For episode-level synopses, we also added a full-show summary to the prompt to provide context from previous episodes; we observe summaries substantially improve performance when compared to non-summary context variants, so we report only summary-based variants.Our takeaways from this experiment are:Cascade improves quality. Our primary metric, Recall-FAIL improves on both show and episode level synopses, with a limited impact on Recall-PASS. In other words, we now catch more Gold FAIL synopses without sacrificing the reliability of our PASS verdicts.Cascade is cheaper. Cascade cuts total cost by 52.4% on the show-level dataset. Cascade (with summary) is also 15% cheaper than the current (no summary) holistic pipeline on episodic dataset.Cascade’s P50 latency increases with respect to the holistic baseline. Even so, this remains within what we consider a reasonable range for factuality judgment.Simple tweaks aren’t enough. Increasing reasoning effort makes the factuality checker too lenient, while using a smaller model makes it too strict — neither addresses the underlying problems of the holistic baseline.Summary context matters for episodic tasks. Without a full-show summary, the model tends to over-fail because it lacks the context to determine whether a detail from the episode summary fits the broader storyline.Alignment with Human RationaleSo far, we’ve established that the cascade produces better verdicts: it catches more non-factual synopses and produces more reliable PASS decisions. But are these verdicts correct for the right reasons?To measure this, we use an LLM-as-a-Judge to compare each pipeline’s reasoning against the human rationale on Gold-FAIL (GF) synopses. The judge assigns a Reasoning Similarity Score (RSS) of 0 (dissimilar), 0.5 (partially similar), or 1 (very similar) based on rationale overlap.We observe that cascade is significantly better aligned with human rationale in all cases. This is a big gain — not only is the cascade giving us more accurate factuality verdicts, but it also identifies the same points of contention in the synopsis as a specialized human annotator.Conclusion + Future WorkOverall, our proposed cascade pipeline improves both cost and quality of the existing factuality service:On the cost side, confidence gating lets us avoid unnecessary calls, reducing the average cost of factuality evaluation.On the quality side, two diverse judges allow us to collect complementary informative verdicts, while the Stage-2 judges recheck and correct the assumptions behind uncertain decisions. This results in higher verdict accuracy and substantially better alignment between model and expert annotator reasoning.The cascade gives us a path toward a factuality system that is not just more accurate, but also more interpretable and self-correcting. Some future directions to consider would be:Adding multimodal inputs to help verify claims that text assets alone cannot confirm.Use the rationale from factuality checking to correct the faulty synopsis.Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Netflix] Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing
summary: Serdar Cellat, Yuchen Xie, Bernadette Marcu, Blaid Burgess, Cody Jarrett, Carlos Pereira, Qing Shi, Samuel Carvajal, Manuel Pamplona, Dorothy Jung, Feiko Ritsema, Benjamin Klein, Alex Woo, Eugene Lok, Anna Pulido, Rebecka Swe, Sanford Holsapple, Ranjith Kumar ShettyIntroductionClips in the Netflix mobile app.At Netflix, a crucial part of our mission is ensuring our content looks stunning on any device. Vertical formats are increasingly important for Netflix, as we have 1.2B followers across our social media accounts, and have recently rolled out Clips, our vertical video feed in the Netflix mobile app. Traditionally, creating vertical assets meant editors and producers manually reframed horizontal videos in editing tools, a process that doesn’t scale as our catalog and use cases grow. To support both our in‑app feed and external marketing campaigns at scale, we built an automated multi‑ratio video cropping system, tightly integrated into our internal production tools, that can generate high‑quality vertical and other aspect‑ratio variants with minimal manual effort.Our Video Resizing ApproachConverting cinematic 16:9 footage into mobile‑friendly aspect ratios takes more than a simple center crop. Filmmaking often involves dynamic character blocking and complex camera movement. We need an intelligent “virtual camera” that can follow the key action, respond to how each scene is composed, and produce crops that feel as intentional as the original shot.We address this challenge by framing video resizing as a tracking and temporal optimization problem. Our pipeline processes each asset in three main stages, designed to produce 9:16, 4:5, and 1:1 crops in a single pass, without incurring additional computational overhead.An overview of the three-stage process converting horizontal footage into mobile aspect ratios.Shot Detection and SplittingFirst, we segment the video into atomic shots using a neural‑network–based shot boundary detector. In many cases, shots contain multiple characters conversing on opposite sides of the frame. To better handle these scenarios, we use an Active Speaker Detection based approach to logically split a single continuous shot into multiple sub‑shots. This allows our virtual camera to cut and re-focus on different speakers as the conversation flows. Our Active Speaker Detection leverages an internal face detector and LipFlap to reliably identify active speakers in both live‑action and animated titles.Shot splitting via Active Speaker Detection. The magenta box represents the dynamic vertical crop.Focus Region DiscoveryOnce shots and sub‑shots are defined, we identify the most important region in each frame. We combine face detections with visual saliency maps to filter and prioritize the faces that should be in focus. In scenes with multiple characters, we further rank faces using signals such as active speaker status and relative size. Our model aggregates these cues with shot‑level content understanding to establish a continuous “focus region” for the virtual camera.Blue box shows the focus region around the primary character for reframing.Temporal ReframingOnce we’ve established the focus region, the next challenge is deciding how the crop should move over time. Tracking the focus region on a strict frame-by-frame basis would produce a shaky, distracting viewing experience, so we apply a set of heuristics that consider how the focus region moves over the course of a shot. When its displacement is small, we lock a static crop window that consistently covers the relevant area. When there is significant motion, we compute a dynamic tracking window and smooth its path so that any panning feels intentional and cinematic.The vertical crop (magenta box) follows the character’s movement with a smooth panning path.Tooling and Workflow IntegrationWe integrated the resizing algorithm directly into our internal Clips tool, so editors and producers can access it as part of their existing workflow. The interface enables them to automatically generate multiple aspect‑ratio versions of a clip with smart reframing. A unified in‑app module provides intuitive shot‑reframing controls, allowing users to review the algorithm’s crops, and quickly make targeted adjustments where needed.For more complex shots or custom campaigns, producers can export the resizing parameters as XML and load them directly into external timeline editors such as Adobe Premiere. This allows agencies and external partners to start from the algorithm’s framing decisions instead of recreating crops manually or relying on tools like Premiere’s Auto Reframe. In our internal test, our resizing algorithm outperforms Auto Reframe on a curated evaluation set, so the XML export effectively brings those higher‑quality crops into external workflows. By bringing automated resizing and manual refinement into a single place, this pipeline significantly reduces production time and manual effort while preserving creative control.Video resizing interface with reframing controlsConclusionOur work on multi-ratio video resizing is one step in a broader effort to make content creation more scalable, without compromising creative intent. By pairing algorithm-driven reframing with editor-friendly tools, we’ve reduced the time teams spend on repetitive resizing tasks and unlocked faster experimentation across mobile feeds and marketing campaigns. As we continue to broaden these capabilities to new formats and workflows, our goal remains the same: to give creatives more time to tell great stories, and to deliver a consistently high-quality viewing experience for our members and fans.Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Netflix] Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes
summary: By Roberto Perez Alcolea, Java Platform TeamQuasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decisionAt Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed.The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it.Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next:Does any consumer still call this method?Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations?Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact?Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign?At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds.Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally.We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions:What changed in the library’s public API?Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed?The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing.From API Changes to Consumer ImpactExisting techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive.Quasar builds on SCIP, an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently.On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change.During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings through its REST and GraphQL APIs and MCP server; follow-up usage queries provide dependency-version breakdowns and source locations. A separate compatibility-impact assessment can also follow implementations and their callers when a producer supplies a changed JVM symbol.Consider this simplified API change:public interface Client {- Result getLegacyValue(Request request);+ Result getValue(Request request, Options options);}For a detailed compatibility-impact assessment of this removal, a producer-side tool supplies the old method descriptor. Quasar constructs its canonical symbol identity. This abridged excerpt from the direct-reference portion of Quasar’s Amazon Athena query shows the essential match:SELECT c.change_id, 'DIRECT_REFERENCE' AS evidence_kind, r.scm_type, r.org, r.repo, r.dep_version, r.file_pathFROM requested_changes cJOIN quasar.symbol_refs r ON r.symbol_canonical = c.target_canonicalrequested_changes contains the API changes submitted by the producer. The SQL excerpt finds repositories that call the removed method. Quasar also checks implementations and calls through them, so it can count each affected repository once. It returns sample dependency versions and file locations to help investigate the result.For the Client change, this tells the producer which repositories still use getLegacyValue, which versions they use, and where some of those calls occur. That helps the producer decide whether to coordinate a migration before removing the method.Bringing the Analysis Before ReleaseVersion-to-version comparison is valuable when planning an upgrade or writing a migration guide. Producers benefit even more when feedback arrives during code review.For pull-request analysis, Quasar stores API definition snapshots keyed by commit. Given a base and head commit, it classifies symbols as added, removed, or signature-modified. Removals and modifications then become candidates for consumer-impact analysis.An incompatible change is not automatically a high-risk change. Quasar reports the observed impact so the producer can decide what to do; it does not enforce a release policy. “No references observed” means only that Quasar found none in the indexed population. Reflection, configuration, dynamic loading, stale branches, or incomplete indexing can hide consumers. The result needs to show whether the requested commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated.Pull-request review requires indexed snapshots for the exact base and head commits. If either is unavailable, Quasar reports that it cannot compare them; it does not substitute a default-branch snapshot. This keeps a missing comparison from looking like a clean API diff.Return to our Client change. This illustrative report brings together signals available through Quasar's API comparison, consumer-usage queries, and library-level criticality. It is not a literal response from one API:{ "change": "REMOVED", "symbol": "Client#getLegacyValue(Request)", "affectedRepositories": 137, "versionDistribution": , "sampleConsumerLocations":  }, { "repository": "client-wrapper", "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/client/ClientAdapter.java", "lines":  } ], "libraryCriticality": { "tier": 1, "basis": "highest-tier downstream application" }, "comparison": { "baseShaFound": true, "headShaFound": true }}An impact report shows 137 affected repositories distributed across library versions 4.2.1, 4.1.7, and 3.9.4.The repository count is symbol-specific: in this example, 137 indexed repositories refer to the removed method. The version distribution reveals a dominant cohort on 4.2.1 and a smaller long tail still on 3.9.4. A producer can inspect affected repositories and retrieve indexed file paths, with line numbers where the index provides them. The JSON shows only two sample locations to keep the example readable. The filePath and lines shape mirrors Quasar's query contract. The tier is broader context about the library, inherited from its highest-criticality downstream application; it does not imply that all 137 callers are Tier 1.Together, those signals change the producer’s plan. Instead of merging the removal and waiting for failures, the producer can retain and deprecate the old method, publish a migration path, coordinate a broader migration, and track the long-tail versions before removal. File paths and available line numbers turn that scope into a concrete work list for engineers or coding agents. The same API diff paired with weak or stale evidence would lead to a different action: refresh the indexes before deciding. The value is not merely detecting the removal; it is choosing a proportionate next step.A pre-release workflow enriches API changes with consumer impact and evidence quality before the producer decides how to proceedA Polyglot Foundation with SCIPThe shared SCIP format also lets Quasar index several language ecosystems. Each language indexer resolves its own code, while Quasar can use the resulting symbol identities to find references across repositories.Conceptually, client-lib indexes Client#getLegacyValue(Request) as a definition, while checkout-service indexes a reference to the same symbol. Quasar can then connect the library API to its consumer across repositories.Language-specific indexers emit SCIP definitions, references, and relationships into Quasar’s shared semantic graph.Relationships are especially useful when generated code separates the API a producer owns from the symbols consumers invoke. For example, Quasar can trace a Protobuf definition through its generated Java members to the repositories that use them, even when consumer code never names the .proto element.SCIP records symbols and their references; it does not determine whether an API change violates an ecosystem’s compatibility rules. Today, Quasar compares indexed JVM and Protobuf API definitions and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java to find affected repositories. A separate JVM compatibility-impact path uses breaks identified by a producer-side tool to query affected repositories. Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust support usage queries, but Quasar does not yet assess their breaking API changes.Moving Risk Assessment EarlierToday, Quasar surfaces API-change findings on pull requests, including observed consumer counts and confidence. Producers can use its other queries to inspect dependency versions and source locations, with library criticality as broader context. Together, those signals support a decision before merge.We want to move that context earlier. An agent writing library code should recognize when it is changing a public symbol and consult Quasar before the change becomes a pull request. Quasar’s APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration provide an access path, but access alone does not create awareness. The coding workflow must also recognize public API edits so the agent knows when to query impact and when to involve the producer.Today Quasar assesses risk on a pull request. The future workflow gives agents consumer-impact context while they write code, before the pull request is opened.Earlier guidance will not replace pull-request analysis. The PR assessment will still verify the concrete diff and catch changes that were not recognized during coding. Coverage, freshness, ambiguity, unsupported platforms, and truncation must travel through both checks in machine-readable form. An agent should not turn “no observed usages in the available index” into “safe to remove.”Today, agents can query Quasar through MCP when prompted. We are working toward making that context part of the coding workflow, then using identified call sites to prepare migration changes. Quasar supplies semantic evidence, an agent reduces migration toil, and the library producer remains responsible for API and release decisions.What We LearnedBuilding this workflow led us to four practical lessons.Separate compatibility from reach. A removed method can break the API contract even when Quasar finds no callers. A list of affected repositories and their library versions shows the migration work ahead. Producers need both signals to choose a release path.Make the evidence inspectable. A repository count is more useful with sample call sites and a version breakdown. The result also needs to show which commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated. Otherwise, “no usage found” can be mistaken for proof that nobody is affected.Keep usage and compatibility separate across languages. SCIP lets Quasar find symbol references in several ecosystems. Deciding whether an API change is breaking requires compatibility rules or a trusted producer-side signal for that ecosystem.Bring evidence to the producer while choices are open. Pull-request findings can prompt a producer to retain an API, publish a migration path, or coordinate consumers before merge. Moving the same evidence into the coding workflow could shape the edit earlier. After release, it still helps locate consumers that need to migrate.Today, Quasar indexes JVM, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust code for cross-repository usage analysis. It compares JVM APIs and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java. Producers can review change findings through Quasar’s REST and GraphQL APIs or its MCP server, then investigate affected repositories and call sites. We are extending this foundation toward more ecosystem-specific compatibility checks, deeper code-review integration, and agent-assisted consumer migrations that keep release approval with the producer.Quasar is internal to Netflix, but the pattern is portable: index code semantically, retain API definitions, compare them at the point of change, query affected consumers, and report the quality of the evidence. Library producers need more than a compatibility verdict. They need to know who may be affected and have enough time to act before release.A huge thank you to the Java Platform team at Netflix. Their expertise, collaboration, and support made this work possibleRelated TalksFrom Lag to Lightning: Transforming Dependency Update Timelines explores how Netflix shortened dependency-update timelines.Netflix’s Journey to Confident Automated Code Changes discusses building confidence in automated changes at scale.Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Docker] Docker patches Java4Shell and the NGINX HTTP/2 with Docker Hardened Images
summary: OpenJDK and Oracle disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) on November 17, and NGINX released fixes for two HTTP/2 flaws the next day. Docker began publishing fixed images for both in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog starting that same day. What we know about Java4Shell is that it’s a memory-corruption bug in the Java runtime that can let an attacker with no credentials run code inside a Java application. Many container images contain a Java runtime, including application images that bundle their own, so it affects teams well beyond the ones that write Java. Docker Hardened Images are the trusted foundation your applications should run on, because a flaw in the runtime inside an image is fixed only when that image is rebuilt, and Docker rebuilds its hardened images as soon as upstream fixes become available. Fixed images for the Amazon Corretto, SapMachine and Azul Zulu runtimes and for NGINX are in the catalog today, with Eclipse Temurin following as soon as Adoptium completes its fixed builds. TL;DR Affected: Java 17.0.6 and later, including Java 21, 25, 26 and 27, from every OpenJDK vendor. Only on some hardware: the bug is reachable only when the JVM runs on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI. The same image can be exposed on one host and not on another. Fixes are arriving vendor by vendor. Corretto, SapMachine and Zulu builds in DHI are fixed. Temurin, which many DHI application images use, is not released yet. Check the version the runtime reports. A tag or a recent rebuild date does not tell you which Java build is inside an image. java -version does. Until your image runs a fixed build, start Java with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. Set it yourself and check that it took effect. Make sure it reaches every JVM, not only the first one. The second half of this post shows how. The NGINX HTTP/2 flaws are fixed in the catalog. The Docker Hardened Images for NGINX are rebuilt on NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. Pull the image again, or move a pinned tag to one of those versions, and redeploy. What the vulnerability is To decode Base64 quickly, the HotSpot JVM uses a hand-written routine built on AVX-512 instructions. That routine miscalculates a length when the input ends in unexpected padding and writes up to 62 bytes past the end of a buffer on the Java heap. Calif, the researchers who found it, turned that into heap disclosure and remote code execution. They demonstrated code execution before authentication against default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and after authentication against Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. They note there is no universal exploit: each application needs its own, and they have not published those. As of November 18 there are no public reports of exploitation in the wild. Oracle rates the issue 8.1 (High) under CVSS 3.1. The researchers rate it 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0. CISA has issued an alert urging immediate patching. How to find out if you’re exposed Java version. The JVM is 17.0.6 or later and does not yet include the fix. The fixed OpenJDK versions are 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1. Vendors add their own suffixes, but in the builds we checked, the build string printed by java -version contains one of those four numbers when the runtime is fixed. CPU. The host is x86-64 and supports AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Xeon from Ice Lake onward, AMD EPYC and Ryzen from Zen 4 onward. ARM64 hosts are not affected. Reachability. Data an attacker controls reaches Java’s Base64 decoder. That includes Authorization headers, tokens, SAML messages and file uploads. A Java client that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server is also in scope. For anything that accepts network input, assume this is true. All three of these must be true To check a host’s CPU, run this on the host or Kubernetes node. Hardened runtime images have no shell, so it will not run inside the container. grep -m1 ‘^flags’ /proc/cpuinfo | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep -E ‘^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$’ The host is affected if all four flags are printed. Two other ways to check, for when a shell on the node is hard to get. Ask the JVM. This works in hardened images: docker run –rm –entrypoint java <image> -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -w UseAVX UseAVX = 3 means the JVM is using AVX-512 on that host. Treat the host as affected until the full check says otherwise. A value of 0 to 2 means AVX-512 is not in use. On ARM64 nothing is printed. The answer applies only to the host the command ran on. Ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type shows the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true. Check build runners and CI workers as well. They run Java, and they talk to the network. Ask the JVM. This works in hardened images: docker run –rm –entrypoint java <image> -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -w UseAVX UseAVX = 3 means the JVM is using AVX-512 on that host. Treat the host as affected until the full check says otherwise. A value of 0 to 2 means AVX-512 is not in use. On ARM64 nothing is printed. The answer applies only to the host the command ran on. Ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type shows the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true. Check build runners and CI workers as well. They run Java, and they talk to the network. Where Docker Hardened Images stand Java runtime in DHI DHI status Amazon Corretto 17, 21, 25, 27 Fixed. The published images report 17.0.21.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 25.0.5.1.2 and 27.0.1.1.4. SapMachine 21, 25, 27 Fixed. The published images report 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2 and 27.0.1.1+4. Azul Zulu 17, 21, 25, 27 Fixed. The published Zulu images we checked report 17.0.21.1+2, 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2 and 27.0.1.1+4. Eclipse Temurin 17, 21, 25, 27 Waiting for Adoptium to complete its release. On November 18 Adoptium had published 27.0.1.1+4 for x86-64 Linux only. 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1 and 25.0.5.1 were still in testing. Adoptium tracks progress in adoptium/temurin#326. Our published images still report 17.0.21+9, 21.0.13+9, 25.0.5+8 and 27.0.1.0.2+1, which are vulnerable. Java 26 (any vendor) Java 26 reached end of support in September 2026, so no fix is expected from any vendor, and it is not among the fixed lines in the OpenJDK advisory. If you run it, treat it as affected and keep the flag set. We recommend moving to Java 25 or updating to Java 27. If you cannot migrate yet, ask us whether Extended Lifecycle Support can cover your version. It is the Docker Hardened Images Enterprise add-on for software past its upstream end of life. Java 8 and 11 Not affected by this CVE and no action is needed for it. The same November update fixes other issues in these lines, so update when new images arrive. Application images that bundle Java, such as Keycloak, Jenkins, Kafka, Elasticsearch and Solr They follow the bundled runtime, which for many of them is Temurin, and they are rebuilt once the runtime they use is fixed. Until then, set the flag yourself. Set the mitigation flag yourself on every JVM that is still waiting for a fixed runtime, and check what each image already sets before you do. Treat the flag as a stopgap, because a JVM is protected only if the flag reaches it when it starts, and a deployment setting or a start script can override it or drop it. A fixed runtime is the only thing that closes the issue, so move to the fixed image as soon as it is published. Next Steps: If you are not running Docker Hardened Images yet The CPU check and the mitigation flag in the steps below apply to any image that runs a HotSpot-based OpenJDK build. The version strings in this post come from Docker Hardened Images, so for an image from another source, confirm the fixed build in that source’s advisory. The fixed build can only come from whoever builds your image, because the Java runtime and the system packages your application runs on come from the image underneath it. That dependency is why a hardened image is a necessary step toward a trusted software supply chain. With Docker Hardened Images, tracking each vendor’s fix and rebuilding on it is work Docker does for you. The images are minimal and secure by default, and they are built to serve as a trusted and verifiable upstream for your builds. You can move a service onto one by following the migration guide. If you have Docker Hardened Images deployed 1. Find the Java in your deployments, by version. Look for DHI Java runtime images, DHI application images that bundle Java, and your own images built on either. Include JVMs you add in your own layers. Ask each runtime for its version. This works on hardened images, which have no shell:docker run –rm –entrypoint java <image> -versionCompare the result with the fixed versions above. Temurin-21.0.13+9 is vulnerable. Corretto-21.0.13.1.2 is fixed.Do not rely on a vulnerability scan alone for this. The public vulnerability databases were still incomplete for this CVE on November 18. Set the flag. For most deployments, set JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS on the container:docker run -e JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=”-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics” <your-image>env: – name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS value: “-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics”Three cases need more care, and the next section covers them: images that already set Java option variables (our FIPS images do), environments that also run Java 8, and anything that starts more than one JVM.Prefer this flag to -XX:UseAVX=2, the other published mitigation. UseAVX does not exist on ARM64, and a JVM given it there will not start. Applications that decode very large volumes of Base64 may run slower with the flag. Test before a wide rollout.The flag addresses this CVE only. The same OpenJDK release fixes nine other CVEs, including two rated 7.4 that affect every Java line from 8 to 27. Only the fixed image addresses those. Restart, then verify. The flag is read only at JVM startup. It cannot be changed in a running JVM, so every JVM has to be restarted. Then look for this line in the container log:Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics Check your CPUs, and keep checking. Run the CPU command on every node pool. A cluster with mixed instance types can schedule the same pod onto an affected node tomorrow. If any node in a pool is affected, treat the workload as affected. Reduce exposure. Restrict network access to Java services that do not need to be public, starting with identity, CI/CD and collaboration systems. The researchers note that a proxy which buffers whole request bodies gets in the way of some of their exploits but not all of them, so do not count on it. Watch for crashes, and think about secrets. A failed attempt can crash the JVM. In the container log a crash starts like this:# A fatal error has been detected by the Java Runtime Environment:## SIGSEGV (0xb) at pc=0x…, pid=1, tid=…The JVM also writes a report named hs_err_pid<pid>.log inside the container. That file is gone when the container is replaced, which in Kubernetes happens straight away. To keep it, point -XX:ErrorFile at a mounted volume. The malformed input is also rejected with an IllegalArgumentException, so a burst of Base64 decoding errors in an application’s log is worth a look. Neither signal is reliable, and a service that stays up is not proof that nothing happened.The researchers could read the Java heap before they could run code. If you have reason to believe an exposed JVM on affected hardware was attacked, treat the keys, tokens and passwords it held as disclosed, and rotate them. Making the flag reach every JVM A container often runs more than one JVM, for example when a build tool forks a JVM for tests, an application server starts helper processes or a CI agent starts a JVM for every build step. The flag protects only the JVMs that receive it, and the variable most people reach for first is JAVA_OPTS, which Java does not read at all. Where you put the flag What reads it Child JVMs get it? Watch out for JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS The JVM itself, however it is started. Includes javac, keytool and other JDK tools. Yes, through the inherited environment A Java 8 JVM that sees it refuses to start. Some DHI FIPS images already set this variable. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS Only the java launcher, Java 9 and later Yes, when the child is started with java Not read by javac, keytool or other JDK tools. DHI FIPS images set it. Java 8 ignores it. The java command line That one JVM No Nothing downstream inherits it. JAVA_OPTS, JENKINS_JAVA_OPTS, MAVEN_OPTS, ES_JAVA_OPTS and similar A start script, which copies the value onto one java command line No Each script has its own rules. If nothing in the image reads the variable, it does nothing. Five rules follow from that table. We tested each on DHI images. JAVA_OPTS only works where a script reads it. With JAVA_OPTS=”-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics” set and a plain java command, the intrinsic stays on. No warning is printed. A flag on the command line stops at that process. We started a JVM with the flag on its command line and had it start a second JVM. The child ran with the intrinsic on. With JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS in the environment, the child ran with it off. A child started with a cleared environment gets nothing, whichever variable you use. Check what the image already sets before you set anything. In Docker and Kubernetes, your value replaces the image’s value. It is not appended. docker inspect –format ‘{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}’ <image> \ | grep -E ‘^(JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS|JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS)=’ Our FIPS images use these variables to configure the FIPS provider. dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-fips sets both. When we replaced its JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS with only the flag, the JVM started normally, but the org.bouncycastle.fips.approved_only property was gone. Nothing warned us. If the command prints a value, copy it and add the flag at the end: env: – name: JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS value: “<the existing value from the image> -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics” Not every FIPS image uses the same variables, so run the check for each image. Keep JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS away from Java 8. Java 8 is not affected and does not know the flag: Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:-UseBASE64IntrinsicsUnrecognized VM option ‘UseBASE64Intrinsics’Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine. Adding -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions to the variable does not help on Java 8. Where Java 8 shares an environment with a newer Java, either scope the variable to the containers that need it or use JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS, which Java 8 ignores. Java 11 accepts the flag, so it is harmless there. Verify the process, not the environment. Running java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version inside a container starts a new JVM. It tells you what the environment gives a new JVM, not what the JVM already serving traffic was started with. For the running process, use the startup log line. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS prints one too, starting with NOTE: Picked up. In an image that includes the JDK you can also ask the process directly: jcmd <pid> VM.flags | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics The answer must be -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. If the flag reached the JVM through an environment variable, it will not show in the process’s command line, so ps is not a reliable check. Some applications discard these variables on purpose. Elasticsearch’s start script, for example, ignores JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and expects ES_JAVA_OPTS. Check your application’s documentation. When the fixed images arrive Pull the new image and redeploy. Four things catch people out: The tag may not change. dhi.io/amazoncorretto:21.0.13 now reports the fixed Corretto-21.0.13.1.2, a newer build than the tag name suggests. A tag cannot tell you which build you are running. java -version can. Kubernetes may not pull. With imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent, the default for every tag except latest, a node that already holds the old image under that tag keeps using it, even after a restart. Deploy by digest, or set the policy to Always for this rollout. Mirrors lag. If you copy DHI into your own registry, the fix arrives when your mirror next syncs. Your own images need a rebuild. An image built FROM a DHI Java image keeps the old runtime until you rebuild and redeploy it. Then confirm with java -version that what is running reports a fixed build. After that, remove the flag from every place you set it. The NGINX HTTP/2 flaws are fixed in the same catalog The day after Java4Shell, NGINX released fixes for two memory errors in the way it handles HTTP/2 connections, tracked as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. A crafted request can crash a worker process, and where an attacker gets past the operating system’s memory protections it can run code inside that worker. Both flaws need HTTP/2 to be enabled on the server, and the same releases fix other NGINX issues that do not depend on HTTP/2, so update either way. The Docker Hardened Images for NGINX were rebuilt on NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 and published on November 18, the same day as the upstream release. To patch, pull the image again and redeploy, and move any tag pinned to an older exact version to a fixed one. nginx -v prints the version, and the fixed ones are 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. The notes on pull policy, mirrors and your own images in the section above apply to NGINX images in the same way. Who does what The vulnerable code is in the Java runtime inside the image, and if you are using DHI, shipping the fix becomes our job. Whether that code can be reached in your deployment depends on things an image cannot see: the CPU it is scheduled onto, the options you start it with, the processes it starts, and the traffic you send it. With Docker Hardened Images, Docker will Without Docker Hardened Images Track every Java vendor and ship fixed runtimes in DHI as soon as they are released Track every Java vendor yourself and rebuild your base images on each fixed runtime Tell you which images are fixed and which are still waiting Find out from each vendor which of its builds are fixed Tell you what we know, and update this post Follow the OpenJDK, Oracle and vendor advisories as they change Three jobs stay with you whichever image you run. Pull the fixed images, redeploy, and confirm the Java version that is actually running. Make sure the flag is set on every JVM that is still waiting for a fixed runtime. Know which CPUs your workloads run on, control what can reach your Java services, and patch the JVMs you add yourself. So how many more bullets are you willing to dodge? It was only four weeks ago that the news was PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Calif, the security research team that found Java4Shell and helped find PHP2Shell, says it used AI to find this flaw in about an hour and that the whole effort cost less than $200 in tokens. When a flaw like this can be found and weaponized at that price, it is reasonable to expect more of them. If you lead a team or answer for how your organization builds and ships software, the questions after a week like this one are whether you were exposed and how quickly you can prove you were not. It is imperative to have a trusted foundation in place before the next flaw appears, and Docker Hardened Images is that foundation to adopt. This week Docker began publishing fixed Java and NGINX images to the catalog within a day of each disclosure, with the images still waiting listed in the status table above. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, so you have a record of what it contains and how it was built. The Docker Hardened Images catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, and moving one of your services onto a hardened image typically means changing one line in its Dockerfile. If you are not building on Docker Hardened Images yet, start today.

title: [Engineering at Meta] Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon
summary: Meta’s Reality Labs builds products such as AI glasses. Emulators provide us with a way to scale development and testing without relying on scarce physical hardware. Testing software for non-phone Android devices depends on how closely a virtual device reproduces the software behavior of the physical product. While a lightweight emulator like Goldfish gets you part of the way, differences from the real device can hide bugs until later in development. This lack of fidelity also erodes trust in device emulation, increasing reliance on scarce physical hardware. Cuttlefish is the Android Open Source Project’s (AOSP’s) virtual-device framework for testing Android software against virtual hardware. It boots the same system images as real hardware and runs a realistic software stack against virtual hardware. This enables Cuttlefish to more closely track a physical device’s behavior than a lightweight emulator does. Unfortunately, Cuttlefish is only supported on Linux, and our application and library developers work on Macs with Apple silicon. This forced us to support Goldfish and Cuttlefish side by side. We knew if we could consolidate onto a single Cuttlefish-based platform, we could give all of our developers the benefit of the same high-fidelity virtual device. The challenge was porting the stack to make Cuttlefish run natively on macOS. The Impact of Fragmentation Maintaining dual emulator platforms imposed a heavy operational burden: It drained computing resources, created confusion for developers, and slowed down the emulator team. Every tool required support for two separate platforms, while infrastructure and engineering capacity were divided between them. Furthermore, developers had to choose an emulator target based on how they worked: Goldfish ran everywhere but had less fidelity while Cuttlefish needed Linux. The AOSP mirrors this exact divide: Goldfish targets application developers, whereas Cuttlefish serves Android platform developers. So long as we maintained that division, we would suffer the effects of fragmentation. The Stack and the macOS Gaps Cuttlefish is the orchestration layer, while the component that actually runs the guest OS is a virtual machine monitor (VMM). On Linux, Cuttlefish normally uses crosvm but previously included support for QEMU as an alternative VMM. That integration had become inactive over time. To enable native Apple silicon support on macOS, we revived QEMU support. Many of Cuttlefish’s virtual devices use vhost-user backends, separate processes that provide virtio devices to QEMU over a socket. The architecture is clean, but large parts of it were written with a hard Linux assumption. Three of those assumptions break on macOS. The vhost-user machinery is gated to Linux and won’t build or run. The Apple hypervisor imposes resource limits QEMU didn’t expect. Finally, the native display, build, and signing paths didn’t exist. We tackled all three. The Cuttlefish-on-Mac stack. Cuttlefish orchestrates virtual devices backed by QEMU. The highlighted orange blocks are the Mac-specific work: adding macOS support to vhost-user, increasing memory-region tracking slots in QEMU’s HVF backend, and using the native Cocoa display and code-signing paths. Making vhost-user Portable Beyond Linux The most structurally important changes were in QEMU’s vhost-user path. The frontends, libvhost-user, and the contrib backends such as vhost-user-blk were all gated to Linux. We relaxed those build restrictions so the vhost-user frontends and libraries can build on macOS as well as Linux. This lets Cuttlefish’s device backends hand off to QEMU on a Mac the same way they do on Linux. Without this, the higher-fidelity device model that makes Cuttlefish worth using isn’t available outside Linux. Living Within Hypervisor.framework On Apple silicon, QEMU accelerates through HVF (Hypervisor.framework) instead of KVM. QEMU’s HVF backend did not track enough memory regions for larger Cuttlefish configurations. We increased its tracking-slot count so those configurations could run correctly. A Usable Native Display Local application development requires an interactive display allowing developers to view and engage directly with the virtual device. To enable direct interaction and bypass reliance on the WebRTC interface, we transitioned to QEMU’s native Cocoa display. The changes include: BGRA Pixel Format Support: Enables accurate display rendering to eliminate visual artifacts on Apple silicon. Mouse-Click-as-Touch: Translates pointer actions into touch input for interacting with touchscreen devices. Custom Geometry Options: Adds the -g flag to graphic_console_init for display configuration. We also enabled the unstable Rutabaga structs needed to match the Rust-side graphics ABI in gfxstream/rutabaga configurations. Building and Signing on Apple Silicon Finally, there was the build and packaging work: initial Darwin build support, building QEMU for arm64 on macOS, and toolchain fixes. The macOS builds also needed the JIT entitlement in addition to support for code signing and notarization. On the Cuttlefish side, we added macOS host support so the framework’s orchestration builds and runs on a Mac instead of assuming a Linux host. The Benefits By moving to a unified platform, we cut maintenance requirements, reduced infrastructure needs, eliminated redundant tooling, enhanced fidelity, and ensured developers run the exact same Cuttlefish virtual devices used across CI. A single platform also made it easier to support capabilities on a shared stack, including: Bluetooth pairing and connectivity. Wi-Fi. Cellular. 3D graphics. Over-the-air (OTA) update testing to exercise over-the-air update flows against a virtual device. Fastboot. Snapshotting to save and restore device state in CI and development flows. Beyond supporting Reality Labs engineers, this identical virtual device is shared with external developers building for our ecosystem. This alignment guarantees that third-party teams test against the exact same Cuttlefish-based platform we use to develop and validate the OS itself. With AI agents playing a growing role in Android development, validation execution and runtime behavior is just as essential as code generation. Virtual devices empower both engineers and automated agents to operate concurrently within isolated environments, facilitating application execution and rapid iteration. By enabling instant state resets and repeated test runs, teams eliminate dependencies on shared physical hardware and prevent workflow interruptions. Ultimately, high-fidelity emulation ensures these continuous feedback loops are both rapid and meaningful. Giving Back to the Community Although we built this for development within Reality Labs, the macOS support is useful beyond our products. We’re sharing our work with the community so other developers can build on the QEMU and AOSP foundations that enabled our work. We’re distributing the work in two parts: qemu-wearables: a Meta-maintained fork of QEMU carrying our commits. cuttlefish-wearables: a set of patch files, with instructions for patching Android/AOSP. The repositories contain our QEMU changes and the Cuttlefish patch series, along with build and patch-application instructions. We’re also exploring ways to contribute these changes upstream to QEMU and AOSP. In the meantime, developers can use our fork and patch set. Acknowledgements This project relies on the foundations laid by the QEMU and Cuttlefish/AOSP communities. We are particularly grateful for the vsock-user implementation created by Stefano Garzarella, which directly enabled our macOS integration. Special thanks also go to Olya Arkhangelskaia and Tom Care at Meta for their foundational work bringing Cuttlefish to macOS, and to Jeffrey Effendy for improvements to the native Mac developer experience and subsequent productization work.
